== Biography ==
Robert Elder was born in 1903 in Tehorny, County Antrim, Ireland.  He was the son of [[Elder-3240|Isaac Elder]] and [[Simpson-15883|Jane Simpson]]. <ref> Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht, Ireland. Civil Records. https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie. Marriage: 
:Name	ISAAC ELDER
:Date of Birth	1877
:Group Registration ID	10204669
:SR District/Reg Area	Ballymoney
:Sex	N/R
:Mother's Birth Surname	N/R 
https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/birth_returns/births_1877/03026/2108870.pdf</ref>

Robert's father Isaac Elder died of tuberculosis in 1910 at Tehorny, Rasharkin, County Antrim. 

In the 1911 Ireland census, Robert Alexander Elder was age 7 living at Tehorny, Rasharkin, County Antrim with his mother Jane Elliott (sic) (38), a widow, and his siblings from Jane's first marriage Samuel James Elliott (21) and Sarah J M Elliott (19).<ref>National Archives of Ireland. 1911 Ireland census: http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1911/Antrim/Killoquin__Upper/Tehorny/130409/</ref>

[[Category: Tehorny Townland, Rasharkin Parish, County Antrim]]
== Biography ==
Isaac Elder was born in 1877 in Gortereghy, County Antrim, Ireland.  He was the son of Robert Elder and Jane Calderwood.<ref> Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht, Ireland. Civil Records. https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie. Marriage: 
:Name	ISAAC ELDER
:Date of Birth	1877
:Group Registration ID	10204669
:SR District/Reg Area	Ballymoney
:Sex	N/R
:Mother's Birth Surname	N/R 
https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/birth_returns/births_1877/03026/2108870.pdf</ref>

In the 1901 Ireland census, Isaac Elder was age 23, a farm servant living at Tehorny, Rasharkin, County Antrim in the household of Jane Elliott (38), a widow, and her children Henry Elliott (13), Samuel Elliott (11) and Sarah Elliott (9).<ref>National Archives of Ireland. 1901 Ireland census: http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1901/Antrim/Killoquin_North/Tehorney/946758/</ref>

Isaac Elder married Jane Elliott on 19 February 1903 at Portglenone Presbyterian Church, Portglenone, County Antrim, Ireland.<ref>Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht, Ireland. Civil Records. https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie. Marriage: 
:Party 1 Name	ISAAC ELDER
:Party 2 Name	JANE ELLIOTT
:Date of Event	19 February 1903
:Group Registration ID	1869475
:SR District/Reg Area	Ballymena 
https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1903/10220/5720267a.pdf</ref> 

Isaac and Jane Elder had a son, Robert Alexander Elder (b.1903).

Isaac Elder died of tuberculosis in 1910 at Tehorny, Rasharkin, County Antrim.<ref> Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht, Ireland. Civil Records. https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie. Marriage: 
:Name	ISAAC EIDER
:Date of Death	1910
:Group Registration ID	5109096
:SR District/Reg Area	Ballymoney
:Deceased Age at Death	33 
https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/deaths_returns/deaths_1910/05430/4518107.pdf</ref> 

Isaac Elder was buried at Rasharkin Presbyterian Church graveyard, Rasharkin, County Antrim.

== Research Note ==
It appears that Jane (Simpson) Elliott may have been the cousin of Isaac Elder, which may explain why he was working on her farm in 1901.  Isaac's mother, Jane Calderwood, was the daughter of Alexander Calderwood of Glenbuck.  Jane Simpson's mother was Sarah Calderwood, who was the daughter of an Alexander Calderwood.  He may have been the same man as Jane's father.  Alexander Calderwood of Glenbuck died in 1886 and his will mentioned daughters called Jane and Sarah.

Alexander Calderwood of Glenbuck, d.1886

== Biography ==
Jane Simpson was born in 1859 in County Antrim, Ireland, probably at Tehorny.  She is the daughter of [[Simpson-14277|Alexander Simpson]]<ref name="marr"/> and [[Calderwood-393|Sarah Calderwood]]. 

Jane Simpson married Henry Elliott on 12 August 1884 at Rasharkin Presbyterian Church, Rasharkin, County Antrim, Ireland.<ref name="marr">Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht, Ireland. Civil Records. https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie. Marriage: 
:Party 1 Name	HENRY ELLIOTT
:Party 2 Name	JANE SIMPSON
:Date of Event	12 August 1884
:Group Registration ID	2296460
:SR District/Reg Area	Ballymoney
https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1884/10906/5983840.pdf</ref>

Henry and Jane Elliott had four children: William Alexander Elliott (1885–1893), Henry John Elliott (b. 1887), Samuel James Elliott (b. 1889), Sarah Margretta Elliott (b.1891).

Jane's husband Henry died of heart failure in 1890.  Jane's brother Robert had been present at the time.  Her son William died in 1893.  His death was registered by Jane's mother Sarah Simpson.

In the 1901 Ireland census, Jane Elliott, a widow, was age 38 living at Tehorny, Rasharkin, County Antrim with her children Henry Elliott (13), Samuel Elliott (11) and Sarah Elliott (9).  Also Isaac Elder (23), farm servant.<ref>National Archives of Ireland. 1901 Ireland census: http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1901/Antrim/Killoquin_North/Tehorney/946758/</ref>

Jane Elliott married Isaac Elder on 19 February 1903 at Portglenone Presbyterian Church, Portglenone, County Antrim, Ireland.<ref>Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht, Ireland. Civil Records. https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie. Marriage: 
:Party 1 Name	ISAAC ELDER
:Party 2 Name	JANE ELLIOTT
:Date of Event	19 February 1903
:Group Registration ID	1869475
:SR District/Reg Area	Ballymena 
https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1903/10220/5720267a.pdf</ref>  Jane's brother Alexander Simpson was one of the witnesses.

Isaac and Jane Elder had a son, Robert Alexander Elder (b.1903).

Isaac Elder died of tuberculosis in 1910 at Tehorny, Rasharkin, County Antrim. 

In the 1911 Ireland census, Jane Elliott (sic), a widow, was age 48 living at Tehorny, Rasharkin, County Antrim with her children Samuel James Elliott (21), Sarah J M Elliott (19) and Robert Al Elder (7).<ref>National Archives of Ireland. 1911 Ireland census: http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1911/Antrim/Killoquin__Upper/Tehorny/130409/</ref>

Jane Elder died in 1937 age 77.<ref>Public Record Office of Northern Ireland. Will Calendars. https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/services/search-will-calendars.

Effects £86 5s.</ref>  She was buried at Rasharkin Presbyterian Church, Rasharkin, County Antrim  with her two husbands and two of her sons. Her gravestone has an incorrect death date of 23 January 1927.

Elder-7251.Name: Elder-7251
Elder-7251.bio:
{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==

'''Robert Elder''' was born about 1831, probably in County Antrim. His birth estimate is based on his reported age of 40 at marriage.

On 14 June 1871 Robert married [[Glasgow-3167|Mary Glasgow]] in the Ballymoney registration district. The original register describes him as a 40-year-old bachelor and farmer and names his father as '''[[Elder-7300|Nathaniel Elder]], farmer'''. Mary was a 28-year-old spinster residing at Lisnagaver, daughter of [[Glasgow-951|Alexander Glasgow]], farmer.<ref name="ElderGlasgow1871">General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register, marriage of Robert Elder and Mary Glasgow, 14 June 1871; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1871/11341/8162804.pdf digital image].</ref>

The Lisnagaver valuation revision books later show Robert succeeding Alexander Glasgow as occupier of lot 25, containing 8 acres 2 roods 10 perches. This supports continuity between the marriage family and the Lisnagaver Glasgow household but does not by itself establish Robert’s death date.<ref name="LisnagaverRevision25">Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, valuation revision books for Lisnagaver, Rasharkin parish, PRONI VAL/12/B/4/16C and VAL/12/B/4/16D, lot 25; [https://apps.proni.gov.uk/Val12B/Search.aspx PRONI search and image viewer].</ref>

=== Family and later records ===

The 1901 census records Robert's widow [[Glasgow-3167|Mary Elder]] at Gortahar with their children [[Elder-7302|Mary]], [[Elder-7303|Robert J.]] and [[Elder-7304|Jane M.]].<ref name="Census1901">1901 Census of Ireland, Gortahar, Rasharkin, County Antrim, Mary Elder household; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QPB2-KNM2 indexed record].</ref> In 1911 Robert J. headed the continuing household with his mother, sister Jane and nephew [[Elder-7305|Samuel Glasgow Elder]].<ref name="Census1911">1911 Census of Ireland, Gortahar, Rasharkin, County Antrim, Robert J. Elder household; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QYHR-52T2 indexed record].</ref>

A published transcription of the First Garvagh Presbyterian register records the marriage of [[Elder-7301|William Elder]] and [[McMaster-2595|Ellen J. McMaster]] on 6 September 1864. William's father was [[Elder-7300|Nathaniel Elder]], farmer, and Robert Elder was a witness.<ref name="WilliamMarriage1864">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/GarvaghP1/Marriages/1845-1889marr.html First Garvagh Presbyterian Church marriages, 1845–1889], entry 110, William Elder and Ellen J. McMaster, 6 September 1864.</ref> The common father, occupation, locality and Robert's role as witness make William a likely brother, although the identification remains qualified pending the original register and further family evidence.

A Robert Elder aged 64 whose death was registered at Ballymoney in the fourth quarter of 1894 is a strong candidate for this man and would explain Mary's widowed status in 1901.<ref name="Death1894">Ireland civil registration death index, Robert Elder, Ballymoney, October–December 1894, vol. 1, p. 100; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FTZP-9M6 indexed record].</ref> The original death entry is required before the identification is treated as proved.

== Research Notes ==

Nathaniel's birth date is a generation estimate only. No record presently identifies his wife, birth, death or residence. He should not be confused with same-name Elders without a record-level connection.

A Nathaniel Elder occupied land at Annaghgad in Creggan parish, County Armagh, in the 1827 tithe applotment book.<ref name="AnnaghgadTithe1827">National Archives of Ireland, ''Tithe Applotment Book'', Annaghgad, Creggan parish, County Armagh, 1827; [https://titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie/reels/tab//004587426/004587426_00034.pdf digital image].</ref> No record links that occupier to Robert or William Elder, whose known records belong to the north Antrim–south Derry network. He remains a separate same-name candidate and should not be merged or attached without a direct bridge.

{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==

'''Mary Glasgow''' was born about 1843, probably in County Antrim. Her birth estimate is based on her reported age of 28 at marriage.

On 14 June 1871 she married [[Elder-7251|Robert Elder]] in the Ballymoney registration district. The original register describes Mary as a 28-year-old spinster residing at Lisnagaver and explicitly names her father as [[Glasgow-951|“Alexr. Glasgow,” farmer]]. Robert was a 40-year-old bachelor and farmer, son of Nathaniel Elder.<ref name="ElderGlasgow1871">General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register, marriage of Robert Elder and Mary Glasgow, 14 June 1871; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1871/11341/8162804.pdf digital image].</ref>

The valuation revision books provide independent locality evidence. Robert Elder later replaced Alexander Glasgow as occupier of Alexander’s Lisnagaver holding, lot 25, containing 8 acres 2 roods 10 perches.<ref name="LisnagaverRevision25">Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, valuation revision books for Lisnagaver, Rasharkin parish, PRONI VAL/12/B/4/16C and VAL/12/B/4/16D, lot 25; [https://apps.proni.gov.uk/Val12B/Search.aspx PRONI search and image viewer].</ref>

Mary was present at Gortahar on 27 February 1892 when she registered the death of her mother, [[McCaughan-222|Mary Glasgow]]. The death register identifies the informant as the deceased woman’s daughter, Mary Elder.<ref name="MaryGlasgowDeath1892">General Register Office of Ireland, civil death register, death of Mary Glasgow, 27 February 1892, Gortahar; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1892/06049/4723532.pdf digital image].</ref> Mary Elder therefore died after that date.

=== Gortahar household ===

The 1901 census index records Mary Elder, aged 60, widowed, Presbyterian and a farmer, as head of a Gortahar household with children [[Elder-7302|Mary]], [[Elder-7303|Robert J.]] and [[Elder-7304|Jane M.]].<ref name="ElderCensus1901">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QPB2-KNM2 FamilySearch, Ireland census index], Mary Elder household, Gortahar, County Antrim, 1901.</ref> In 1911 her son [[Elder-7303|Robert J. Elder]] headed the continuing Gortahar household with his widowed mother Mary, sister [[Elder-7304|Jane M. Elder]] and a two-year-old nephew displayed as “Samuel Glasgow.”<ref name="ElderCensus1911">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QYHR-52T2 FamilySearch, Ireland census index], Robert J. Elder household, Gortahar, 1911; individual entry for [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QYHG-YHMM Mary Elder].</ref>

The nephew was registered as '''[[Elder-7305|Samuel Glasgow Elder]]''' at Ballymoney in the third quarter of 1908; Glasgow was his middle name rather than his surname.<ref name="SamuelGlasgowElder1908">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FBP3-95M Ireland civil registration birth index], Samuel Glasgow Elder, Ballymoney, July–September 1908, vol. 1, p. 111.</ref> The continuing residence and relationships, together with Samuel's Glasgow middle name, make this household a high-confidence continuation of the family formed by Mary and Robert Elder. Samuel's parents remain unidentified.

A Robert Elder aged 64 whose death was registered at Ballymoney in the fourth quarter of 1894 is a strong candidate for Mary's husband and would explain her widowed status in 1901.<ref name="RobertElderDeath1894">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FTZP-9M6 Ireland civil registration death index], Robert Elder, Ballymoney, October–December 1894, vol. 1, p. 100.</ref> The original death entry is still required before the identification is treated as proved.

=== Disambiguation ===

This profile was previously identified with Maryan Glasgow, aged 17 in the 1851 Glenleslie household of [[Glasgow-1022|John Glasgow]].<ref name="Glenleslie1851">National Archives of Ireland, ''Census of Ireland, 1851'', Glenleslie, Dunaghy, Kilconway, County Antrim, house 21, household of John Glasgow.</ref> The original 1871 marriage register instead says that Robert Elder’s wife was 28 and names her father as Alexander Glasgow. The Glenleslie Maryan should therefore not be used to assign this Mary a birth in 1834 or John Glasgow as grandfather.

A Mary Jane Elder died at Lisnagaver on 11 June 1897, aged 65, with John Elder, described as her son, as informant.<ref name="MaryElderDeath1897">General Register Office of Ireland, civil death register, death of Mary Jane Elder, 11 June 1897, Lisnagaver; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1897/05858/4660280.pdf digital image].</ref> That age conflicts with Mary’s reported age at marriage, and the record has not been linked to Robert Elder’s family. It remains a same-name candidate rather than this profile’s death.

The former suggestion that she was [[Glasgow-2045|Mary Ann (Glasgow) Bell]] is also unsupported. No primary record found gives Robert Elder’s wife the middle name Ann.
A marriage for Mary Glasgow and Elder was registered on 14 June 1871 in the Magherafelt district.<ref>[https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/marriage GRONI civil marriage index], 14 June 1871, Magherafelt district, M/1871/N1/1863/1/179.</ref>

Glasgow-1509.Name: Glasgow-1509
Glasgow-1509.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
'''James Glasgow''' was reportedly born in '''1737'''. A Larne or Kilwaughter congregational record is said to contain an entry for a James, son of [[Glasgow-1499|Hugh Glasgow]], at '''New Town, Larne''', in that year.

The original congregational entry, or a reliable full transcription, has not yet been cited on this profile. The exact birth date, place and identification of Hugh as James’s father should therefore be treated as probable rather than conclusively established.

James was a '''ropemaker''' at Larne, County Antrim. A lease dated 10 September 1760, registered on 24 November 1763, describes him as a ropemaker of Belfast and leases him a marked-out ropewalk at Gardenmore in Larne for thirty-one years from 1 November 1760. He agreed to build a house at the south end of the ropewalk.<ref name="Ropewalk1760">Registry of Deeds transcript, lease dated 10 September 1760 and registered 24 November 1763, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-S7XZ-8 FamilySearch image].</ref>

On 28 March 1768 James, described as a ropemaker of the Old Town of Larne, assigned the plot, workhouse and remainder of the same lease to John Hill for £50. The matching commencement date and rent identify it as the 1760 ropewalk.<ref name="Ropewalk1768">Registry of Deeds transcript, assignment dated 28 March 1768, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-DDXW FamilySearch image].</ref>


A memorial at '''St Cedma’s Church, Larne''', is reported to record James Glasgow with the dates '''1737–1802''' and to name his wife as '''Janet Shutter'''. A photograph or complete reliable transcription of the monument should be cited before the exact dates and marriage are treated as fully verified.

James is reported to have died in '''1802'''.

An Irish probate-index transcription records a '''James Glasgow of Larne''' in the Diocese of Belfast in '''1803'''.<ref>Irish probate index transcription supplied July 2026, entry for James Glasgow, Diocese of Belfast, residence Larne, 1803.</ref>

The agreement in name and residence, together with probate in the year after the reported death, makes this a strong match to the man commemorated at St Cedma’s.

The 1803 entry should be understood as a probate or estate event. It does not replace the reported 1802 death year. Probate occurring in the year following death would be ordinary.

The probate entry establishes Larne as James’s recorded residence during the estate proceedings. It does not by itself prove that Larne was his place of death.

=== Wife and family ===

James’s wife is reported on the St Cedma’s memorial as '''Janet Shutter'''.

The complete inscription should be obtained and cited because the memorial may also contain:

* Janet’s dates;
* the date or duration of the marriage;
* children buried in the same plot;
* other Glasgow relatives; or
* wording clarifying whether the monument was erected by descendants.

No inspected baptismal, marriage, will or probate record currently cited on this profile names James’s children.

The 1803 probate record may be important. An original will, administration bond or surviving abstract could identify:

* Janet as his widow;
* sons or daughters;
* married daughters or sons-in-law;
* executors or administrators;
* business partners;
* property at Larne or Blackcave; or
* other relatives.

== Research Notes ==
=== Identification and evidence ===

The following records probably concern the same man:

* the James, son of Hugh Glasgow, reportedly recorded at New Town or Larne in 1737;
* James Glasgow, ropemaker, documented in the 1760 ropewalk lease and 1768 assignment;
* James Glasgow commemorated at St Cedma’s with dates 1737–1802 and wife Janet Shutter; and
* James Glasgow of Larne whose estate entered Belfast probate in 1803.

The chronology and repeated Larne association make this identification plausible and probably correct.

The strongest direct contemporary evidence presently cited is the 1760 ropewalk lease and its 1768 assignment. The baptism and memorial evidence still require complete source citations, and the probate index does not name James’s father or wife.

The profile should therefore distinguish between:

* directly documented facts, including James’s ropemaking and Larne residence in the 1760–1773 records;
* strong identity matches, including the 1803 probate entry; and
* reported but not yet fully exposed evidence, including the 1737 congregational entry and St Cedma’s memorial.

=== Ropemaker evidence and identity distinction ===

A Registry of Deeds memorial dated 14 May 1766 also names James Glasgow, ropemaker of Larne, as a witness.<ref>[https://www.irishdeedsindex.net/mem.php?memorial=204122 Registry of Deeds Index Project, memorial 204122], deed dated 14 May 1766.</ref> In 1773 Mr James Glasgow of Larne, gentleman, swore that he was aged upwards of thirty, placing his birth before 27 October 1743.<ref name="Larne1773">Registry of Deeds memorial and affidavit, sworn 27 October 1773, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-M72W-M FamilySearch image].</ref> Alexander Holmes's 1799 will later identifies a Larne occupant as James Glasgow, roper. The repeated occupation and place form a coherent sequence.

The 1768 assignment was witnessed by a '''different''' James Glasgow who was expressly described as a tanner. A 1778 mortgage and the 1786 Blackcave lease continue that tanner sequence and fit [[Glasgow-3991|James Glasgow (about 1747–1812)]]. The two tradesmen should not be conflated.

The reported 1737 congregational occurrence and the present uncertain placement under [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]] remain competing parentage hypotheses until the original entry or another relationship record is inspected.

=== Research priorities ===

Further research should obtain:

* the original or fullest available congregational entry for the 1737 James, son of Hugh Glasgow;
* the name of the congregation and exact wording of that entry;
* a photograph or complete transcription of the St Cedma’s memorial;
* evidence supporting Janet Shutter’s identity and marriage to James;
* the exact nature of the 1803 Belfast probate entry;
* the original will, administration record or bond, if it survives;
* a Betham or other pre-destruction abstract of the estate;
* names of beneficiaries, executors, witnesses or sureties; and
* records identifying any children of James and Janet.

=== Research conclusion ===

James Glasgow was directly recorded as a ropemaker in the 1760 Larne ropewalk lease, the 1766 memorial and the 1768 assignment.

The 1803 Belfast probate entry for James Glasgow of Larne is a strong match to the man reportedly commemorated at St Cedma’s with dates 1737–1802. It supports Larne as his probate residence while remaining consistent with death in 1802.

The reported identification of his wife as Janet Shutter and his father as Hugh Glasgow is plausible, but the complete memorial and congregational record should be cited before those relationships and the exact dates are treated as certain.

=== Current Larne reconstruction ===

James is securely the Belfast/Larne ropemaker in the 1760 Gardenmore ropewalk lease and its 1768 assignment, and the 1773 affidavit places that adult James at Larne and over thirty. The 1768 document separately calls its witness James Glasgow a tanner; that is a different occupational record group, probably [[Glasgow-3991|James Glasgow]], and does not change this James's occupation. The original 1784 lease registered in 1790 has now been inspected: its witness is explicitly a tanner and belongs to the separate occupational sequence probably represented by [[Glasgow-3991|James Glasgow]]. James is a plausible earlier-generation candidate in the Larne reconstruction, including as a possible father of [[Glasgow-3902|Adam Glasgow]] and possible kin of [[Glasgow-3904|older Alexander Glasgow]], but no record yet makes either relationship. His 1762 marriage to Janet Shutter postdates Adam's estimated 1758 birth, so Janet cannot be called Adam's mother. A William Glasgow, merchant, witnessed the 1760 lease, but is not yet definitely [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]].<ref name="LarneCurrent">Registry of Deeds memorials for the 1760 lease, 1768 assignment and 1773 affidavit, cited above.</ref>

=== Additional source context ===

These contextual and comparison sources supplement the individual record assessments above; they do not supply a missing parental statement.
* Related profile: [[Glasgow-1509]].
<ref name="Retained2">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJ4-4SJF Registry of Deeds, 1784 transaction registered in 1790: James Glasgow, tanner; sworn 17 August and registered 23 August 1790].</ref>


A lease dated 14 January 1784 was witnessed by James Glasgow of Larne, '''tanner''', with Samuel Drummond, merchant, and James Farries, writing clerk. James’s affidavit was sworn 17 August 1790; the memorial was registered on 23 August. The original reads “Tanner”, resolving an earlier automated “Turner” reading. This strengthens the occupational sequence, without independently naming his family.<ref name="Tanner1784">Registry of Deeds, memorial 278037, lease 14 January 1784, sworn 17 August and registered 23 August 1790, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJ4-4SJF FamilySearch image 437], original inspected 21 September 2026. The online collection label 1734–1736 does not describe this image’s date.</ref>

=== Newtown title succession: identities unresolved ===

An 1874 deed recites a lease to James Glasgow dated 2 October 1779 and its renewal to Anne Glasgow and Jane Glasgow on 25 February 1832. The north-side Newtown property, formerly John English’s, adjoined a tenement formerly Hugh Glasgow’s. This documents succession to a lease, but does not call the women James’s daughters or identify which James held it. The monument wife Jane of [[Glasgow-3991|James Glasgow]] died in 1820 and cannot automatically be the 1832 Jane. [[Glasgow-3992|Ann Glasgow]], whose monument gives a May 1832 death, is only a candidate for Anne; the original renewal is needed.<ref name="Newtown1874">Registry of Deeds, Antrim to John Mulvenna, indenture 25 March 1874, registered 24 August 1874, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CS54-77Q4-H FamilySearch image 475], recital inspected in the original; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CS54-77QC-T continuation image 476].</ref>

29027908.Name: Glasgow-1505
29027908.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==
'''William Glasgow''' was an adult member of the Larne and
Kilwaughter Presbyterian congregation by 1739/40.

The congregation's session accounts record William handling money
received from use of the mortcloth on 17 February 1739/40, in
October 1741 and on 29 December 1743.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184109/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/TheirStory2.html]

These entries cannot concern [[Glasgow-3326|William Glasgow]], born
in 1730, who was only about nine to thirteen years old. They establish
that a separate, older William Glasgow was present in the Larne
congregation.

William's date of birth is unknown. A compiled family reconstruction
associates him with a St Cedma's gravestone and gives a birth year of
about 1708. The same reconstruction elsewhere reports conflicting
tombstone-derived years of 1699 and 1708. No photograph or complete
transcription of the memorial has yet been inspected.

A probate index contains an entry for '''William Glasgow of Larne'''
in 1783. This record cannot presently be assigned securely to this
William because the younger William born in 1730 was also an adult
in the Larne area. The year 1783 should not therefore be treated as
This William's proved death year.

The compiled reconstruction implies that William had an eldest son
named '''James'''. It does not provide a baptism, date, mother's name,
will, deed or complete gravestone inscription identifying that son.
James may remain attached as an uncertain child and working hypothesis.
Given the estimated dates, a grandson or later descendant may be more
likely than a direct son; the attachment must not be presented as proved.

The reconstruction is internally inconsistent concerning a later
James Glasgow born about 1775. Its numbered family list places that
James on the same gravestone as the William born in 1730, rather than
This older William. The shared memorial does not itself establish a
father-and-son relationship.

No inspected contemporary record currently identifies William's wife.

William has been described as a son of [[Glasgow-1502|Robert Glasgow]]
and a brother of [[Glasgow-1504|James Glasgow]]. No inspected baptism,
will, deed, marriage settlement or gravestone transcription proves
either relationship. His description as an uncle of James's son
William is consequently also uncertain.


=== Larne leases and later proof of execution ===

A Registry of Deeds memorial records a lease dated 10 March 1736 from the Earl of Antrim to William Glasgow and [[Glasgow-1499|Hugh Glasgow]] of Larne for two tenements in Newtown of Larne. The lease names no relationship between William and Hugh. Its measuring lives were members of the royal family rather than members of the Glasgow family.<ref name="ROD1736">Registry of Deeds, memorial 63221, lease dated 10 March 1736, Earl of Antrim to William and Hugh Glasgow of Larne; registered 10 April 1738. Original image inspected 21 September 2026. [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSN1-FXR2 FamilySearch image].</ref>

A separate Earl of Antrim lease made in 1737 names William Glasgow of Larne as tenant of a house and garden in Old Town of Larne, on the north side of the street leading from Newtown toward the mill.<ref name="ROD1737">Registry of Deeds, memorial of Earl of Antrim lease to William Glasgow of Larne, made in 1737 and registered in 1739. [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-S3FM-8 FamilySearch image]. The automated transcript obscures part of the original date, so the image should be checked before publishing a verbatim transcription.</ref>

Most importantly, William Glasgow of Larne, described as a gentleman, witnessed a deed dated 19 April 1744 and personally proved its execution at Larne on 6 January 1775.<ref name="ROD1744">Registry of Deeds, memorial of deed dated 19 April 1744, with affidavit of William Glasgow at Larne on 6 January 1775. [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-C674 FamilySearch image].</ref> This directly carries an adult William of Larne from 1744 to 1775. It is much more consistent with this older William than with [[Glasgow-3326|William Glasgow]], reportedly born in 1730 and therefore only about fourteen in 1744. None of these deeds identifies William's parents, wife or children.

=== Joint lessors named in a 1757 assignment ===

A deed poll dated 4 June 1757, Matthew Stewart of Carncastle, farmer, to Robert Rainey of Larne, weaver, concerned a conditional assignment for £20 of Stewart's interest in a lease granted by [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-1499|Hugh Glasgow]] of Larne. The original memorial does not date their head lease or describe the holding sufficiently to identify it with the 1736 Newtown tenements.<ref name="JointLessors1757">Registry of Deeds, memorial 159181, manuscript pp. 473–474, deed dated 4 June 1757, registered 26 May 1761; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJM-MJX4 FamilySearch image 257, opening] and [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJM-MJP6 image 258, continuation], original images inspected 21 September 2026.</ref>

The joint names and Larne locality strongly support association with these lessees, but the record names no Glasgow relative or relationship between William and Hugh. Neither Glasgow executed this assignment; its registration in 1761 does not prove that either was then living. The separate 1751 and 1767 endorsements to the 1736 lease remain unexamined and may identify replacement lives.<ref>PRONI D2977/3A/4/81/72A, 1736 William and Hugh Glasgow lease with 1751 and 1767 endorsements; [https://apps.proni.gov.uk/eCatNI_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI eCatalogue], catalogue description only.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
The early session-account dates include:

* adult by 17 February 1739/40;
* living on 29 December 1743.

The dates about 1708 and 1783 should remain uncertain until the full
St Cedma's inscription or another direct record is examined.

The Larne and Kilwaughter Presbyterian collection at PRONI,
reference MIC/1B/6, includes baptisms from 1720 to 1769, marriages
from 1721 to 1769, session minutes and poor accounts. These records
should be searched for:

* a marriage of William Glasgow between approximately 1725 and 1740;
* baptisms of children of William Glasgow;
* a son James;
* any entry naming William's wife;
* references distinguishing the older William from William born
  in 1730.
  
== Possible Descendants ==

The precise identity of William's children has not been established from
an inspected baptism, will or deed. A plausible descendant reconstruction
can nevertheless be formed from Larne occupational, gravestone and family
naming evidence.

A possible son was '''James Glasgow''', a ropemaker who was already an
adult by 1760/61. An advertisement in the Belfast News-Letter of
2 January 1761 announced that “James Glasgow, Rope maker from Belfast”
had erected a ropewalk at Larne.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 2 January 1761,
advertisement by James Glasgow, ropemaker.</ref>

A compiled family chronology reports that James married '''Janet Shutter'''
in 1762 and had a son William about 1763.<ref>
[https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/Timeline.html
Chronology of the Glasgow family in Northern Ireland].
</ref>

Alexander Holmes's will, dated 5 June 1799, refers to a field held with
James Glasgow and to houses occupied by “James Glasgow, Roper” in Old
Town, Larne.<ref>Registry of Deeds Abstracts of Wills, vol. III,
abstract of the will of Alexander Holmes of Larne, dated 5 June 1799;
RD 527/136/345729; PRONI T681, p.344.</ref>

No inspected record presently names the ropemaker's father. His age,
occupation and location make him a possible son of this William, but the
relationship remains uncertain.

The ropemaker's probable son was '''William Glasgow''', born about 1763
and died 5 October 1816. A published transcription of his gravestone in
Larne Parish Churchyard records his wife Elizabeth and daughters Jane
Shutter, Eliza and Mary.<ref>Francis Joseph Bigger and Herbert Hughes,
“Armorial Sculptured Stones of the County Antrim,” ''Ulster Journal of
Archaeology'', vol. VI (1900), p.47.</ref>

The inscription records:

* Jane Shutter Glasgow, died 21 April 1799 aged nine months;
* William Glasgow, died 5 October 1816 aged 53;
* his wife Elizabeth, died 17 September 1832 aged 60;
* their daughter Eliza, died 25 April 1839 aged 37; and
* their daughter Mary, died 18 October 1844 aged 37.

The name '''Jane Shutter Glasgow''' provides significant evidence that
William was connected with James Glasgow and Janet Shutter. The compiled
chronology identifies William's wife as Elizabeth Stewart of Corran and
records a daughter Elizabeth on 30 August 1802. This daughter may have
been the Eliza named on the gravestone.

James Glasgow, born about 1773/75 and currently attached as William's
uncertain son, may instead have belonged to this later generation. If
The ropemaker James was William's son, James born about 1773/75 would
probably have been William's grandson. The existing uncertain attachment
is retained as a working hypothesis pending identification of the
reported shared gravestone or another family record.

The chronology's identification of the ropemaker as a son of Hugh Glasgow
appears problematic. A published transcription of Hugh's family stone
records his son James as dying on 14 April 1812 aged 64, implying birth
about 1748. He would have been too young to establish the ropewalk in
1761 or marry in 1762. The chronology may therefore have combined two
different men named James Glasgow.

== Research Notes: Parentage and Larne Associations ==

William's parentage has not been proved. The present attachment to Robert
Glasgow is derived from the existing family tree; no inspected baptism, will,
deed or congregational minute names Robert as William's father.

A published transcript of the Larne and Kilwaughter congregational accounts
records that in 1734 the congregation's mortcloth or funeral pall was lodged
with “William Glasgow Major”. Accounts relating to the pall continued until
1759. This is a plausible early occurrence of the present William, although
The entry names no relatives and does not by itself establish identity.<ref>
Classon Porter, “Congregational Memoirs—Larne and Kilwaughter,”
''The Christian Unitarian'', vol. 3 (1864), p. 230.</ref>

Registry of Deeds memorial 62131, concerning a deed dated 10 March 1736,
describes William Glasgow as an adjoining occupier at Larne.<ref>Registry of
Deeds, memorial 62131, vol. 84, p. 481, deed dated 10 March 1736.</ref>

A separate Earl of Antrim lease from March 1736 leased New Town of Larne
tenements jointly to William Glasgow and Hugh Glasgow, both of Larne.<ref>
Registry of Deeds, memorial 63221; PRONI D300/2/1/100/3A-B.</ref> Related
lease endorsements survive under PRONI D2977/3A/4/81/72A. The joint tenancy
proves a close property association but does not state that William and Hugh
were brothers.

The surviving congregational extracts for 1699–1700 distinguish John Glasgow
senior of Kilwaughter, Robert Glasgow of the South Side and James Glasgow,
who was appointed overseer for Kilwaughter. No family relationship between
these men is stated.<ref>Classon Porter, “Congregational Memoirs—Larne and
Kilwaughter,” ''The Christian Unitarian'', vols. 2–3 (1863–1864),
transcript of the congregational records for 1699–1700.</ref>

The Connor diocesan probate index records William Glasgow of Larne in 1783. This is a possible match, not a secure identification: more than one adult William Glasgow was associated with Larne. PRONI reports that the original documents do not survive; the index supplies no relatives or exact death date. The estate year must not be treated as this William's proved death year.<ref>[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI Name Search], Connor diocesan probate index, William Glasgow, Larne, 1783.</ref>

Hugh, James, William and the younger Robert Glasgow should therefore be
treated as members of an East Antrim research cluster rather than proved
siblings unless a direct relationship record is found.

=== Unidentified William Glasgow, deed witness in 1772 ===
A lease dated 12 May 1772 from John Miller, currier of Gardenmore in Old Town of Larne, to David Drennan, weaver, names Wm Glasgow, David Dickey and James Fairies, all of Larne, as witnesses. Either [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]] or [[Glasgow-3326|William Glasgow]] could be this witness; the deed gives no age, occupation or relative to distinguish them. The son William named in the trust clause is Drennan's son, not a Glasgow relationship. Registration on 9 November 1784 does not prove that the witness William Glasgow was still alive then.<ref>Registry of Deeds, Miller to Drennan, lease 12 May 1772, registered 9 November 1784, manuscript p. 315, image 166; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-SQLT-3 original image], inspected 21 September 2026.</ref>

46280609.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

William Glasgow of Larne died on '''5 October 1816, aged 53''', according to the published family monument, placing his birth about '''1763'''. His wife [[Stewart-72380|Elizabeth]] died on 17 September 1832, aged 60. Their monument names daughters [[Glasgow-3987|Jane Shutter]], [[Glasgow-3988|Eliza]] and [[Glasgow-3989|Mary]].<ref name="Monument">"Armorial Sculptured Stones of the County Antrim," ''Ulster Journal of Archaeology'', second series, vol. 6 (1900), p. 47, Glasgow inscriptions; [https://archive.org/details/ulsterjournalofa06ulstiala/page/47/mode/1up page image].</ref>

He was probably the son of [[Glasgow-1509|James Glasgow]] and [[Shutter-46|Janet Shutter]], as reported by the derivative family chronology. The distinctive name Jane Shutter supports that reconstruction, but William's original baptism or his surviving will must be read before treating the parentage as proved.


== Research Notes ==

Grant of probate of will of William Glasgow, Larne, Co. Antrim and copy will dated 6 December 1815.<ref>Repository :	Public Record Office for Northern Ireland
PRONI Reference :	D300/1/5/49</ref>

15. William3 Glasgow, b. 1763, 6. 1816, m. Elizabeth, had daughters Jane, Eliza and Mary. Buried St. Cedma's Cemetery in Larne. This could be the William Glasgow, captain of the "William," advertised in the Belfast News Letter 1792-1799. This occupational identification is an unverified suggestion from the inherited chronology; no inspected record connects the captain to this household. 

=== Jane Stewart estate connection, 1823 ===

An assignment of mortgage dated 8 November 1823 names '''Elizabeth Glasgow of Larne, widow, administratrix of Jane Stewart late of Curran, County Antrim, deceased'''. She assigned the mortgage interest to Roger Brown Curry, a Royal Navy lieutenant. The premises were a tenement and garden on the south side of New Town, Larne, 21 feet in front and 189 feet deep, bounded east by the lane to Larne Quay and west by James Mitchell's tenement. William Walsh McNeill, attorney, and James Glasgow, writing clerk, both of Larne, witnessed the assignment.<ref name="Estate1823">Registry of Deeds, memorial 548257, p. 522, assignment of mortgage dated 8 November 1823, registered 17 May 1826; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJ7-9935-Y FamilySearch image 359]. Original image inspected 21 September 2026.</ref>

This widow is a strong candidate for William Glasgow's widow Elizabeth, who survived him from 1816 until 1832, but the deed does not name her late husband. It establishes her authority to administer Jane Stewart's estate, without stating their relationship. The writing clerk's relationship to Elizabeth is also unstated. Jane's administration and the recited mortgage are specific sources to seek next; neither a parent nor a sibling should be assigned from the office of administratrix alone.

== Sources ==

51226662.Name: Glasgow-3986
51226662.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
James was reportedly born about 1773 and died in 1831. His parentage has not been proved. He is currently attached to [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]], but the approximately sixty-five-year gap makes a later generation more likely; the relationship should remain uncertain until a baptism, will or property succession identifies his father.

=== Possible early records ===

A release dated 16 April 1795 concerning garden ground in Newtown of Larne was witnessed by '''James Glasgow of Larne, merchant''', and Charles McGarel, gentleman.<ref name="Merchant1795">Registry of Deeds transcript, release dated 16 April 1795, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-Q9B8-H FamilySearch image].</ref>

An assignment recorded in 1797 concerning a Larne tenement near Charles Dawson Stewart's tanyard includes a witness signature for '''James Glasgow junior'''.<ref name="Junior1797">Registry of Deeds transcript, assignment recorded in 1797, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-Q96R-C FamilySearch image].</ref>

The date, place, merchant designation and use of “junior” fit this James better than the older Larne men. Neither deed names his parents. “Junior” distinguishes him from an older James but does not by itself prove a father-son relationship.

== Research Notes ==
[[Glasgow-4024|James Glasgow of Cookstown (abt.1791-bef.1831)]] was buried at St Luran's on 13 March 1831 aged 40. He is not this Larne man: the reported ages, locality and burial context differ. The profiles should remain separate.

=== Current Larne reconstruction ===

The younger James of Larne remains a provisional identity assembled from the 1795 merchant and 1797 “junior” occurrences. Those records need not identify the same man, and neither names him as the father of [[Glasgow-951|Alexander Glasgow]]. He is nevertheless an age-compatible possible son of [[Glasgow-1509|James Glasgow]] and a possible route to Alexander's generation: an estimated birth about 1773 would allow ordinary fatherhood ages in the early nineteenth century. This is an alternative to the older-Alexander route, not a replacement for the Thomas-family testimony, and Thomas and Daniel must not be assigned to this James merely to make a pedigree. The ropemaker, this possible merchant/junior identity, and the Larne tanner are distinct record groups unless a document joins them. Preserve the existing record citations and state the identity and kinship as provisional.<ref name="YoungerJamesCurrent">The merchant and junior references cited above establish leads, not a father statement for Alexander.</ref>

=== Additional source context ===

These contextual and comparison sources supplement the individual record assessments above; they do not supply a missing parental statement.

Glasgow-3167.bio:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==

'''Mary Glasgow''' was born about 1843, probably in County Antrim. Her birth estimate is based on her reported age of 28 at marriage.

On 14 June 1871 she married [[Elder-7251|Robert Elder]] in the Ballymoney registration district. The original register describes Mary as a 28-year-old spinster residing at Lisnagaver and explicitly names her father as [[Glasgow-951|“Alexr. Glasgow,” farmer]]. Robert was a 40-year-old bachelor and farmer, son of Nathaniel Elder.<ref name="ElderGlasgow1871">General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register, marriage of Robert Elder and Mary Glasgow, 14 June 1871; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1871/11341/8162804.pdf digital image].</ref>

The valuation revision books provide independent locality evidence. Robert Elder later replaced Alexander Glasgow as occupier of Alexander’s Lisnagaver holding, lot 25, containing 8 acres 2 roods 10 perches.<ref name="LisnagaverRevision25">Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, valuation revision books for Lisnagaver, Rasharkin parish, PRONI VAL/12/B/4/16C and VAL/12/B/4/16D, lot 25; [https://apps.proni.gov.uk/Val12B/Search.aspx PRONI search and image viewer].</ref>

Mary was present at Gortahar on 27 February 1892 when she registered the death of her mother, [[McCaughan-222|Mary Glasgow]]. The death register identifies the informant as the deceased woman’s daughter, Mary Elder.<ref name="MaryGlasgowDeath1892">General Register Office of Ireland, civil death register, death of Mary Glasgow, 27 February 1892, Gortahar; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1892/06049/4723532.pdf digital image].</ref> Mary Elder therefore died after that date.

=== Gortahar household ===

The 1901 census index records Mary Elder, aged 60, widowed, Presbyterian and a farmer, as head of a Gortahar household with children [[Elder-7302|Mary]], [[Elder-7303|Robert J.]] and [[Elder-7304|Jane M.]].<ref name="ElderCensus1901">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QPB2-KNM2 FamilySearch, Ireland census index], Mary Elder household, Gortahar, County Antrim, 1901.</ref> In 1911 her son [[Elder-7303|Robert J. Elder]] headed the continuing Gortahar household with his widowed mother Mary, sister [[Elder-7304|Jane M. Elder]] and a two-year-old nephew displayed as “Samuel Glasgow.”<ref name="ElderCensus1911">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QYHR-52T2 FamilySearch, Ireland census index], Robert J. Elder household, Gortahar, 1911; individual entry for [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QYHG-YHMM Mary Elder].</ref>

The nephew was registered as '''[[Elder-7305|Samuel Glasgow Elder]]''' at Ballymoney in the third quarter of 1908; Glasgow was his middle name rather than his surname.<ref name="SamuelGlasgowElder1908">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FBP3-95M Ireland civil registration birth index], Samuel Glasgow Elder, Ballymoney, July–September 1908, vol. 1, p. 111.</ref> The continuing residence and relationships, together with Samuel's Glasgow middle name, make this household a high-confidence continuation of the family formed by Mary and Robert Elder. Samuel's parents remain unidentified.

A Robert Elder aged 64 whose death was registered at Ballymoney in the fourth quarter of 1894 is a strong candidate for Mary's husband and would explain her widowed status in 1901.<ref name="RobertElderDeath1894">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FTZP-9M6 Ireland civil registration death index], Robert Elder, Ballymoney, October–December 1894, vol. 1, p. 100.</ref> The original death entry is still required before the identification is treated as proved.

=== Disambiguation ===

This profile was previously identified with Maryan Glasgow, aged 17 in the 1851 Glenleslie household of [[Glasgow-1022|John Glasgow]].<ref name="Glenleslie1851">National Archives of Ireland, ''Census of Ireland, 1851'', Glenleslie, Dunaghy, Kilconway, County Antrim, house 21, household of John Glasgow.</ref> The original 1871 marriage register instead says that Robert Elder’s wife was 28 and names her father as Alexander Glasgow. The Glenleslie Maryan should therefore not be used to assign this Mary a birth in 1834 or John Glasgow as grandfather.

A Mary Jane Elder died at Lisnagaver on 11 June 1897, aged 65, with John Elder, described as her son, as informant.<ref name="MaryElderDeath1897">General Register Office of Ireland, civil death register, death of Mary Jane Elder, 11 June 1897, Lisnagaver; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1897/05858/4660280.pdf digital image].</ref> That age conflicts with Mary’s reported age at marriage, and the record has not been linked to Robert Elder’s family. It remains a same-name candidate rather than this profile’s death.

The former suggestion that she was [[Glasgow-2045|Mary Ann (Glasgow) Bell]] is also unsupported. No primary record found gives Robert Elder’s wife the middle name Ann.
A marriage for Mary Glasgow and Elder was registered on 14 June 1871 in the Magherafelt district.<ref>[https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/marriage GRONI civil marriage index], 14 June 1871, Magherafelt district, M/1871/N1/1863/1/179.</ref>

{{Ireland Native}}
{{Occupation|image=Wikimedia_Commons_photos-3.jpg|text=was a farmer}}

== Biography ==
=== Alexander’s life in its local setting ===

Alexander’s records describe a family rooted in a small part of County Antrim, with children whose later lives lead beyond it. His clearest surviving household is at Lisnagaver in 1851: an Antrim-born farmer, his wife Mary, and three children. Earlier baptisms recover the beginnings of that family; later marriages and the Elder tenancy connect it to the next generation. The probable Gortahar death completes the broad outline, with the last identity link still open.



==== The places in his life ====


Gortereghy<ref name="Evidencec9d92bcd01">[https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin-upper/gortereghy/ Gortereghy].</ref>, written Gortereagh in the baptism transcription, adjoins Lisnagaver<ref name="Evidence7d988f87c8">[https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/lisnagaver/ Lisnagaver].</ref> to the south. Gortahar<ref name="Evidence10a9c7be48">[https://www.townlands.ie/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/gortahar/ Gortahar].</ref> lies northeast, beyond Moneyleck. They are distinct townlands within the same parish. The map shows approximate modern townland locations, not reconstructed houses or field boundaries.


Both spouses reported first marriage in 1836. Their children’s baptisms place them at Gortereagh in 1837–38 and Lisnagaver by 1843. That suggests a change in the family’s recorded residence between neighbouring townlands; it does not date a move precisely or establish a return to a paternal home. Mary’s possible local family connections deserve investigation in their own right.


The census’s farmer and literate household, the small assessed tenancy and the children’s marriages recover part of Alexander’s circumstances. Later records call him a labourer, and his son-in-law succeeds him on the holding. These changes are compatible with an altered working role as he aged, but their cause is unknown. No inspected source establishes eviction, poverty, or illness-induced retirement. The record sequence and farm analysis distinguish those observations from assumptions about his life.


The following account traces marriage and children, examines the surviving household, then follows the farm, probable death and paternal connections. Missing parentage is one question within that family history.



=== Marriage, Mary’s family and the children ===

Alexander Glasgow and Mary/Molly McCaughan are a documented couple. Their 1851 household reports first marriage in 1836, but no original marriage entry has been located. Rasharkin Presbyterian’s surviving marriage register begins in 1845; First Kilraughts material (Coleraine Family History Society film 197, marriages from 1831) remains a focused alternative.


The marriage-year statement fits the first directly located record sequence. The published transcription of the original Rasharkin Presbyterian register, PRONI MIC1P/292, records the same parental couple at Gortereagh: James Glascaw was born 17 January and baptised 9 February 1837 to Alex and Mary McAughin; an incomplete 1838 entry records a Glascow child of Alex and Molly McAughern; and a later James Glascow was born 9 October 1843 and baptised 7 January 1844 to Alex and Molly McAughern at Lisnagaver. The named transcription can be checked at Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms<ref name="Evidence5574dbd555">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms].</ref>. The register transcription preserves Mary/Molly and McAughin/McAughern. The repeated parental names and residences support their identification with Mary McCaughan while retaining the spellings actually recorded.


The Gortereagh residence is meaningful maternal context, but it is not a parentage proof. The 1834 tithe list includes William and James McCaheran there, a spelling compatible with the recorded McAughin/McAughern/McCaughan forms. This makes a McCaughan family connection a reasonable explanation to test for the newly married couple’s residence, perhaps through Mary's people or a subtenancy. It does not prove that either man was Mary's father, nor that the first son James was named for a maternal grandfather. The 1851 Lisnagaver evidence supplies a more concrete lead: Mary McCaheren, 22, lived with farmer Archibald McCaheren, 60, and Elizabeth in house 31. She is the strongest currently located candidate for the later 1855 bride who named her father as Archy, but that is a separate McCaughan problem. It does not establish Mary Glasgow’s parentage. Likewise, the household of widowed Sarah McCaghrin and grandchildren beside widowed Margaret Elder and children is evidence of a local network of families and neighbours, not an expressed kinship.


The Gortereagh names are recorded in the 1834 Rasharkin tithe book, PRONI '''FIN/5/A/236'''; the 1851 McCaheren and Elder groupings are in Lisnagaver houses 31 and 5. These are separate record observations, not confirmed maternal relatives. See the National Archives census collection<ref name="Evidence0b09d5bb14">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/ National Archives census collection].</ref> and PRONI tithe-book guide<ref name="Evidenceb39783b2e9">[https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/tithe-applotment-books PRONI tithe-book guide].</ref>.

An authenticated FamilySearch search adds a useful comparison lead: a John McCaughan marriage at Rasharkin on 18 March 1851 names '''Jas McCaughan''' as his father, while a separate 1836 Lisnagaver valuation entry names '''Archibald Mccaughan Junr'''. The same search returns Archey and John McCaheran in the 1822–1840 tithe collection. These entries strengthen the conclusion that several similarly named families occupied the area, but their original images and townlands still need checking; none currently proves Mary's parents.<ref name="EvidenceFamilySearchMcCaughan">[https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/record/results?count=100&q.anyPlace=Rasharkin&q.surname=McCaughan FamilySearch Rasharkin McCaughan search], accessed 14 September 2026.</ref>

A separate public Geneanet tree repeats the John McCaughern–Sarah Dysart marriage and proposes a 1872 death for John and a daughter, Mary Anne Jane Rea McCaughern, at Crushybracken about 1858. This supplies a useful descendant-search route, but it is user-submitted derivative material and remains a collateral branch, not evidence for Mary's parents.<ref name="EvidenceGeneanetDysart">[https://pt.geneanet.org/fonds/individus/?go=1&niveaux_1___3869569569__=arbres&niveaux_2___3645179592__=arbres%23utilisateur&nom=MCCAUGHERN&sourcename__0__=bobspree Geneanet McCaughern public tree index], accessed 14 September 2026.</ref>



==== Six children, with different kinds of evidence ====

The parent relationship is documented; the forename and precise birth/baptism dates are not preserved in the transcription. No death date is proved.

Husband Robert Elder’s later occupation of Alexander’s lot and her role at her mother’s 1892 death strengthen the family identification. She is not listed in house 35 in 1851.

|}


Sources: Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism transcription, entries 75, 106 and 203<ref name="Evidence5574dbd555" />, from PRONI '''MIC1P/292'''; 1851 household image<ref name="Evidence96bd10f1c0">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/view-pdf/?doc=007246523_00175&c19=true 1851 household image].</ref>; the civil marriages linked in the record table below. The baptism evidence is a named transcription; the original incomplete 1838 entry still needs inspection. The two James entries represent separate children, not a duplicate caused by a date discrepancy.



==== What the gaps mean ====


The early children are documented separately from their inferred deaths. The table’s reuse-of-name argument does not supply an exact death date. Nor does the incomplete 1838 transcription identify its child as Samuel: an original copy of '''MIC1P/292, entry 106''' is needed to read the missing name and dates.


The transcription has no entries for 1840 or 1841, around Robert’s likely birth. Failure to find his baptism in that transcription is therefore weak evidence against the known parentage: the census and marriage positively establish his father. The missing original marriage, incomplete baptism entry and missing burial records are different gaps and need different searches.


The unnamed child would have been about twelve or thirteen in 1851. No resident, absent-person or household-death entry records that child in the maintained return audit. That omission weighs against an uncomplicated survival-and-emigration reconstruction, but cannot fix a death date or guarantee that the return was complete. The candidate Samuel Glasgow in Michigan was rejected because no American record supplied the required Antrim/parent bridge and the proposal also had to explain this omission. An impossible February date in a later cemetery transcription cannot name the child. The [[Glasgow-3940|child’s assessment]] preserves the comparison.



=== New parentage research: Mary’s McCaughan/McAughern network ===

The current evidence still does '''not''' prove the parents of [[McCaughan-222|Mary (McCaughan) Glasgow]]. The new research separates several local families that had previously risked being merged by surname and locality alone.

* The complete 1851 Rasharkin-derived return contains several relevant households: the older Archibald McCaheren family at Lisnagaver; William McCaheren; Sarah McCaghrin; Mary McCaheren, age 70, recorded as mother-in-law in the John and Margaret Taylor household; and an 11-year-old John McCaughern recorded as a servant/apprentice. None identifies Mary Glasgow, born about 1811, or names her parents.
* The Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism transcription shows distinct McAughern/McAughin households: Eliza McAughern with Thomas at Carnfinton; Archy McAughern with Elizabeth Kilpatrick at Lisnagaver; and James McAughern, son of John and Jane McAuly, at Ballydonly. These records establish a local network, not a single extended family.
* The 1834 tithe material adds Alexr. McCaughan at Unchenagh in Finvoy, while the Drumadarragh family reconstruction identifies John McCaughey/McCahan, farmer, with children including Jane, Margaret, Nancy, James and Sarah. The Gortereghy William and James McCaheran group remains another candidate cluster. None is linked directly to Mary Glasgow.
* A separate National Archives census-search-form result documents Thomas McCaughern/McCaughan of Gortahar with father John McCaughern and mother Mary Gormley. This is a later-generation, parent-documented local family and does not prove Mary’s parentage.
* Authenticated FamilySearch searches for Mary McCaughan, McAughin, McAughern and McCaheren in the relevant Antrim period returned no indexed result. The apparent Alexander–Mary McCaughan hits belong to a different Catholic Culfeightrin/Ballycastle family, including Mary M’caughan’s 7 April 1867 baptism to Alex M’caughan and Cath Quinn. A separate Mary McCaughern–William Marks cluster is also later and unrelated.

The strongest new route is the pre-1831 '''Kilraughts–Dervock Reformed Presbyterian society material''', PRONI '''CR5/32A/1''' (also appearing in related catalogue references as '''CR5/32/1/1/1–2'''). The PRONI guide describes member-by-society lists, baptisms, marriages, deaths, removals and emigrations from about 1804–1831. Since Mary was probably born about 1811, a household or society entry could name her parents. The Kilraughts and Dervock societies operated together until their 1831 division, so both localities must be searched. This manuscript has not yet been inspected; it is a high-priority evidence target, not proof.

'''Current conclusion:''' Mary’s parents remain unknown. The local McCaughan/McAughern network is now better defined, and the Kilraughts–Dervock family lists are the highest-value unresolved route. No parent should be added to Mary’s profile until an original record explicitly connects her to a named household or parent couple.

=== Following the children into adult life ===


==== Robert: the recorded son and the Scottish continuation ====


Robert, aged ten in 1851, is directly recorded as Alexander and Mary’s son in the same Lisnagaver household. His 5 April 1866 marriage to Jane Graham<ref name="Evidence05c8c53b0b">[https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1866/11531/8240963.pdf 5 April 1866 marriage to Jane Graham].</ref> independently calls him a Lisnagaver farmer and names his father Alexander Glasgow, farmer. Those two records make Robert Glasgow-938 the documented child, with estimated birth about 1840–41 from the census and marriage ages. The often repeated exact 6 November 1840 birth date has no identified supporting original. His probable identification with a later Gortereghy valuation occupier is useful local continuity, but that identification is separate from the proved father–son relationship.


Robert’s later family is followed into Glasgow, Scotland, in the maintained account, which cites a 1871 Scottish census index for Robert<ref name="Evidencea991c3602f">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QV9Y-71S6 1871 Scottish census index for Robert].</ref> and an 1881 index for the younger Alexander<ref name="Evidencecfab144f27">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQQ8-5MB 1881 index for the younger Alexander].</ref>. [[Glasgow-937|Alexander Glasgow (Glasgow-937)]], born about 1871, is the next historical generation in that family reconstruction. The Irish census and marriage provide the direct father–son argument for Alexander-951 and Robert; the Scottish continuation relies here on the maintained census references, not newly inspected original images. The copied exact birth date for the younger Alexander had been cited to the same index used for the census, so it is not adopted as an independently verified birth in this account. Exact Scottish address chronology and Robert’s reported 1902 death remain checks on their own originals.


This carries the story beyond the Antrim farm without making every copied detail equally secure. The tested descendant’s confirmed paternal ancestry reaches Alexander-951; the Y-DNA section explains the genetic comparison without listing living generations.


The precise Scottish birth-image leads and the misplaced 1902 death citation are assessed in the next research tests. Neither has yet been inspected; the direct Irish father–son evidence remains secure.



==== James: a strong Michigan candidate, still an open identity ====


The second James, Glasgow-973, has an unusually clear Irish identity: the 1843–44 baptism and his age seven appearance in the 1851 household establish him as Alexander and Mary’s child. His subsequent association with the James Glasgow buried at Tecumseh, Michigan is strong but still unproved. The Michigan household is well reconstructed: the original 1884 Michigan census image<ref name="Evidence13cf3f6b80">[https://michigan.access.preservica.com/uncategorized/IO_eb4d3f94-3c2f-4701-b5bb-c3ecee9ef9b9/ the original 1884 Michigan census image].</ref> gives a forty-year-old Irish-born baggage agent, and the Brookside register identifies the associated wife and daughters. His daughter Minnie’s 1941 death certificate<ref name="Evidence8b5b1f0905">[https://michigan.access.preservica.com/uncategorized/IO_3dab599e-1093-473c-be85-eee5e9b49154/ 1941 death certificate].</ref> reports James as born in County Antrim. That narrows the comparison materially but names neither Alexander nor Mary and gives no Lisnagaver detail. The 1869 original marriage return, naturalisation papers, or a passenger record is still required before the Michigan life becomes Alexander’s son’s biography.



==== Ann: a later marriage and the Nancy problem ====


Ann, Glasgow-438, is likewise direct family evidence. She was aged four in 1851 and her 13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken<ref name="Evidence157ee58a9a">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1876/11181/8097170.pdf 13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken].</ref> calls her a full-age spinster of Lisnagaver and names Alexander Glasgow, labourer, as father. The occupational wording matters because it independently makes the 1888 Gortahar death’s “labourer” compatible with the former Lisnagaver farmer; it is not grounds to split the two men. Ann’s later married surname also means Nancy Glasgow, who reported Alexander’s 1888 death, cannot simply be equated with her. A separate daughter, or another explanation, remains possible.



==== Mary: the daughter whose records connect the households ====


Mary Glasgow-3167 is not in the 1851 return but is securely added by her 14 June 1871 marriage to Robert Elder<ref name="Evidence5782477e56">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1871/11341/8162804.pdf 14 June 1871 marriage to Robert Elder].</ref>: aged 28, resident Lisnagaver, she named Alexander Glasgow, farmer, as father. Her marriage, Robert Elder’s succession to lot 25, and the Gortahar deaths create the high-confidence bridge between the Lisnagaver couple and Mary McCaughan’s later identity. Mary Glasgow’s 17 February 1892 death return<ref name="Evidence6f1ed437a9">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1892/06049/4723532.pdf 17 February 1892 death return].</ref> records daughter Mary Elder as informant. It does not state a maiden surname or husband, and its reported age 89 conflicts with the retained c.1811 estimate; those limits belong beside the identification, not beneath it.


Mary’s later household also contains an instructive name conflict. Her granddaughter’s 1908 birth<ref name="Evidencebe365902e1">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1908/01647/1657700.pdf 1908 birth].</ref> records '''Samuel Elder''', son of Jane Elder, with no father named; the 1911 household<ref name="Evidenceb4f7bd3ba5">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=490671&c20_year=1911 1911 household].</ref> calls him '''Samuel Glasgow'''. The surname is genuinely present in the census, not merely a modern transcription mistake. These records help reconstruct the continuing family, but neither identifies his father. It would be circular to invent a Glasgow father and then use that invented relationship to strengthen Alexander’s ancestry.


Mary’s absence in 1851 is consequently an unresolved location question within a well-supported later family identification. It does not erase the 1871 father statement. Nor does it establish that she was the Maryan in John of Glenleslie’s household: the roughly nine-year conflict between their implied birth years requires explanation, and no located record joins those two identities.

==== The identity chain, in dependency order ====


# The 1851 Lisnagaver house-35 return<ref name="Evidence96bd10f1c0" /> establishes Alexander and wife Mary, both reported aged 40, with children Robert, James and Ann. This is the starting household; its identity does not depend on either Gortahar death.
# Mary Glasgow’s 14 June 1871 marriage<ref name="Evidence5782477e56" /> identifies a 28-year-old Lisnagaver spinster, daughter of Alexander Glasgow, farmer, marrying Robert Elder, 40, farmer of Gortereghy. It directly establishes the bride’s father. Linking that father to the established Lisnagaver household uses name, residence and occupation; the marriage does not name her mother.
# PRONI valuation revisions<ref name="Evidence5c88fa9a83" />, VAL/12/B/4/16C–D, follow Alexander’s removal from '''Lisnagaver lot 25''' and Robert Elder’s subsequent occupation. Succession to the particular holding strengthens the identification of Robert with the daughter’s husband. The book neither declares an inheritance nor records Alexander’s destination or exact death. It supplies a separate administrative connection, not another explicit statement of kinship.
# The 16 September 1878 birth of Jane Matilda Elder<ref name="Evidence5aecbbb88b">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1878/02945/2078820.pdf 16 September 1878 birth of Jane Matilda Elder].</ref> places Robert Elder and Mary, maiden surname '''Glass''', at Gortahar. The spelling is retained as written. The parents and later household continuity support identification with the 1871 couple; the shortened surname alone would be insufficient.
# Mary Glasgow’s death on 17 February 1892<ref name="Evidence6f1ed437a9" />, entry 234, records a widow aged 89 at Gortahar, with '''daughter Mary Elder''' present. That named relationship supplies the strongest connection between the elderly Glasgow woman and the Elder family. With the preceding marriage and household evidence, it supports the high-confidence identification of the widow as [[McCaughan-222|Mary McCaughan (McCaughan-222)]]. It does '''not''' name her deceased husband.
# The 1888 death of a married Alexander Glasgow in the same townland fits the husband of that widow. This last step remains inferential: neither death expressly identifies the other deceased as spouse, and Nancy has not yet been connected independently to the Lisnagaver family.


The 1901<ref name="Evidencee493b88786" /> and 1911<ref name="Evidenceb4f7bd3ba5" /> Elder households strengthen the family continuation. They are not independent sightings of Alexander. Likewise, the two civil deaths cannot first be assumed to concern a married couple and then cited as independent proof of that assumption. Their combined value depends on the independently established Elder connection.

=== Y-DNA: the connection and the competing histories ===

[[Glasgow-951|Alexander Glasgow (Glasgow-951)]] is the project owner’s '''oldest confirmed direct paternal ancestor'''. The documented descent reaches Alexander; his parents remain unknown. A tested male-line descendant has '''Big Y-700 placement R-FT20271''', also found in a tested descendant of [[Glasgow-2738|James J Glasgow (Glasgow-2738)]], born about 1809–10. These are historical ancestors represented by descendant results, not people who were themselves tested. The shared branch establishes paternal genetic kinship between the tested lines. It does not extend either documentary pedigree automatically. FamilyTreeDNA Glasgow project results<ref name="Evidencedb3c53b8e9">[https://www.familytreedna.com/public/Glasgow?iframe=ydna-results-overview FamilyTreeDNA Glasgow project results].</ref>, checked 13 September 2026.

==== What close STR matching can tell us ====


The maintained comparison gives '''genetic distance three at Y-111''' between the Alexander and James J descendant lines. That makes their connection a valuable research priority. It does not mean three generations: STR changes accumulate unevenly, and observed distance is not the number of father-to-son transmissions. FTDNA’s explanation of genetic distance<ref name="Evidencee3eb9bbee5">[https://blog.familytreedna.com/ftdnatip-report/ FTDNA’s explanation of genetic distance].</ref>.


Another Glasgow line is closer on the larger callable Big Y STR comparison. Consequently James J is the nearest comparison on the specified Y-111 panel, not demonstrably Alexander’s nearest genealogical cousin. The inspected August 2026 Block Tree contains no exclusive named downstream branch joining only these two lines. Wider Y-DNA study and comparison evidence.


Brothers, paternal cousins and descendants of more distant collateral branches remain distinguishable historical hypotheses; the present DNA cannot choose among them. Their similar estimated birth years do not locate their common ancestor. A connection through an earlier generation, followed by migration in one branch, remains compatible with the results. A specific migration route is not established. An exact ancestor, date or cousin degree requires evidence connecting the named people, supported where possible by additional independent descendant comparisons.

=== The wider family: proved links and open bridges ===

The Lisnagaver evidence supports a local Glasgow network; it does not yet yield a single reconstructed pedigree. The starting point is the 1851 sequence. House 34<ref name="Evidence2c97cf113b" /> contains John Glasgow, farmer, with wife Margaret and his unmarried brother Samuel, a linen weaver. House 35<ref name="Evidencedea66e5c28" /> contains Alexander and Mary with their children. House 37<ref name="Evidence6c8cd27a9f" /> contains Thomas Glasgow and Mary Ann. A Watters household separates Alexander and Thomas. The layout establishes a small same-surname farming cluster and useful geographic proximity; enumeration order is not a kinship statement or a property map.


John Glasgow-867 and Samuel Glasgow-2908 belong to a specific '''father-John branch'''. John’s original 16 November 1846 marriage<ref name="Evidencef940c7acb4">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cima-3156063 original 16 November 1846 marriage].</ref> names his father as John Glasgow, farmer. The 1851 household expressly calls Samuel John’s brother. That chain directly establishes the brotherhood and names John-867’s father and his occupation. Extending that father statement to Samuel assumes they shared a father; the census does not distinguish full from half brothers. It does '''not''' identify that father with John Glasgow-1022, the older Glenleslie man, and it does not make Alexander another son. The younger John’s memorial says he died in 1895 aged 78, which implies a birth about 1816–17 and makes the candidate Glasgow-1022 less comfortable than an earlier census-age reading alone. Any maintained attachment to John-1022 is an uncertain identification of the father, not an additional record and not evidence for Alexander’s parentage.


The distinction matters because the neighbouring tenancy pattern is tempting but not decisive. The 1834 tithe names Alexander and Robert Glasgow at Lisnagaver, while later valuation lots 24, 25 and 26 are associated with John, Alexander and Thomas under Robert Harvey. Acreage, field-book and adjacency arguments can suggest tenancy succession or a broader network. They cannot establish a biological descent, and Plantation-measure tithe acreage cannot be numerically matched to statute-measure valuation acreage to manufacture an inheritance. The 1836 field book names Robert Glasgow and Archibald McCaughan junior in the house section but does not name Alexander; its land section does not supply occupier names. It therefore cannot decide who lived together, who inherited, or whether Alexander was a brother of John or Thomas.


Thomas Glasgow-987 and Daniel Glasgow-3896 have a stronger relationship argument than Alexander has with either. Daniel’s 1871 will, indexed through the PRONI Wills Calendar<ref name="Evidence968b317eb1">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/willscalendar_ie/willssearch.aspx PRONI Wills Calendar].</ref>, calls the late Thomas his brother and identifies Daniel Neely Glasgow as nephew; Daniel Neely’s 28 June 1888 marriage<ref name="Evidence47f7d35ebe">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1888/10763/5925382.pdf 28 June 1888 marriage].</ref> in turn names Thomas Glasgow, farmer, as his father. Those two records establish Daniel and Thomas as brothers. Thomas’s PRONI calendar administration<ref name="Evidence9c6dade023">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/WillsCalendar_IE/WillsSearch.aspx PRONI calendar administration].</ref> adds that the Lisnagaver farmer died 21 June 1870 and administration went to widow Mary Anne on 7 September. It was an intestate administration, not a will, and it names no parent, sibling or heir beyond the widow. It cannot be used to extend the proved brotherhood into a parentage for Alexander.


Alexander may be a brother or cousin of Thomas and Daniel. Shared locality, associated land, church context and descendant testimony make that a worthwhile research model. No confirmed Y-DNA comparison with an independently documented Thomas or Daniel descendant is supplied in this case. None of those sources says that Alexander was their brother, so the three men are not a proved sibling set. The 2020 correspondence records the older Alexander-and-Rosanna belief, but provides no demonstrably independent parentage source: the correspondent said she ''believed'' Thomas’s parents were Alexander and Rosanna, separately wondered whether the user’s Alexander was Thomas’s brother, and supplied neither a record citation nor usable autosomal-match data. The later FamilySearch Pedigree Resource File entries derive from an Ancestry member tree and conflict even on Rosanna’s reported death day. They show the circulation of a tradition, not its verification.

The Canadian connection is now supported by an explicit transaction.
