== Biography == {{Multiple Births|2}} {{Ireland Native}} Agnes (Montgomery) Todhunter was born about 1838 in Killead, County Antrim, Ireland, daughter of [[Montgomery-16775|Alexander Montgomery]] (1784 - 1877) and [[Neill-2359|Anna Eliza (Neill) Montgomery]] (~1791 - 1875). Her siblings were: #[[Montgomery-17845|Sarah (Montgomery) Moore]] (1813 - 1892) #[[Montgomery-17846|Mary (Montgomery) Muckle]] (1814 - 1896) #[[Montgomery-17886|Margaret (Montgomery) Neill]] (~1817 - 1903) #[[Montgomery-6376|Eliza Swan (Montgomery) Pirrie]] (1820 - 1895) #[[Montgomery-8594|Archibald Montgomery]] (1821 - 1905) #[[Montgomery-17840|Catherine (Montgomery) Carlisle]] (1825 - 1902) #[[Montgomery-17848|Alexander Montgomery Jr]] (1829 - ) Agnes (~22) married [[Todhunter-73|Joseph Todhunter]] (30) (1830 - 1921) on 4 Jun 1861 in the First Presbyterian Meeting House Holyrood, Belfast. Agnes died on 17 Jan 1862 aged ~23. Agnes was born in 1829. She is the daughter of [[Montgomery-17841|Alexander Montgomery]] and [[Neill-2510|Agnes Neill]]. She was the twin sister of Alexander - both of them were baptised on 27 January 1829 in Killead Presbyterian Church, County Antrim when family residence was given as 'Stradhavern'. Agnes married Joseph Todhunter at the Unitarian Church in Holywood, County Down. The announcement was in the Belfast News-Letter on 6 June 1861 in Belfast, Antrim, Northern Ireland. '''1861 Newspaper''': "Newspapers.com", database with images
Belfast News-Letter (Belfast, Antrim, Northern Ireland) 06 Jun 1861, page 3
{{Newspapers.com|121229799}} (accessed 19 March 2023) Her marriage notice in the Belfast Morning News on Friday 7 June 1861 confirms that she was the youngest daughter of Alexander Montgomery of Dundesart Cottage, Crumlin, County Antrim. Died of inflamation of the lungs after premature still-birth of a boy. == Sources == * Baptism record (Killead Presbyterian Church, accessible at PRONI, not available online).

# [[Munnis-25|Robert Munnis]]

In 1901 Margaret Munnis (35) Presbyterian farmer's wife was recorded in the household of her Presbyterian farmer husband William Munnis (31) at Breckagh Stranocum, Antrim, Ireland. The couple's children Nancy (6) a scholar, Annie (4) a scholar, Catherine 2 and John 1 month were also recorded in the household.<ref>'''1901 Census''', "Ireland Census, 1901," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:Q5YV-D8N2 : 11 March 2022), Margaret Munnis in household of William Munnis, Stranocum, County Antrim, Ireland; citing Census, Stranocum, County Antrim, Ireland, 0000077521, Public Record Office of Ireland, Belfast.</ref>

Margaret Munnis passed away from complications of childbirth on 13 February 1905 at Breckagh in the Ballymoney district of County Antrim, Ireland. She left a widower, who was present at her death and a young family. <ref>'''Death''', [https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/deaths_returns/deaths_1905/05605/4575820.pdf Irish  Genealogy.ie image] Name	MARGARET MUNNIS, Date of Death	1905, Group Registration ID	4761527, SR District/Reg Area	Ballymoney, Deceased Age at Death	39,</ref>

===Will===
A transcription of the digital copy of the will on the PRONI website: “The will and testament of Neal Anderson of Gortreigh in the County of Antrim. I will and bequeath to my three sons the farm of land which I now occupy. I give to my son Neal Twelve acres on the North side of the Farm and the lower part of the dwelling house. To my son Abraham I give twelve acres adjoining the other together with the upper part of the dwelling house. To my son Robert I give twelve acres on the south side together with the Housing situated thereon. To my daughter Elizabeth I give ten pounds stg and to my daughter Mary I give ten pound stg. To my wife Elizabeth I give ten pound stg. To my daughter Anna I give ten pounds stg. To my daughter Leonora I give one pound stg. To my daughter Sarah I give ten pounds stg. To my daughter Isabella I give ten pounds stg if she claims it. All the above sums each of the Boys are to pay an equal share. But in no case do I allow it to be paid for inside five years from the present date. I hereby allow all my legal debts to be paid by my three sons each an equal share. I give to each of my three sons an equal share of my chattle property.
Neal Anderson X His Mark
Witness Robert Adams, John Deullin”

===Probate===
“Letters of Administration (with the Will annexed) of the personal estate of Neal Anderson late of Gortreighy County Antrim Farmer who died 10 April 1877 at same place were granted at Belfast to Neal Anderson of Gortreighy Farmer one of the Residuary Legatees.”

Elder-3945.bio:
== Biography ==
OVERALL, WHAT I HAVE IS CORRECT.  THERE ARE THREE JOHN ELDER THAT ARE SIMILAR.  ON 1900 Fed census he says he was born in MARCH, 1868.  This is only three year off from Mar 1865 where I found birth record in Dirraw, Antrim, Ireland to parents James and Mary Mcagherin Elder. THIS IS MY STRONGEST TIE THAT THIS IS OUR JOHN ELDER.

I believe born in Antrim,  Ireland @ only immigration of John Elder. In census he says 1888, but searched all records and only John Elder arrived May 16, 1887 o ship Devonia [ Note; some web sites mispell it as Deronidi -I looked at Devonia ship manifest and he is there].  He was age 19 which put DOB about 1867 or 1868 but they frequently did not remember their year of birth.  
Ship sailed from Glascow, Scotland. On ship manifest it says he was from Antrim.

I found a John Elder born 15 Mar 1865 in Dirraw, Antrim, Ireland to James Elder and Mary Mcagherin Elder.  I have a note from Joan Elder McNamara, hand written on a piece of paper, saying John Elder was born 21 March 1865.  {This could have been his baptismal date- only 3 days after birth on March 15]  Also found another son born to same couple there, William Elder Nov. 9, 1869 in Dirraw, Antrim but this is different DOB than Elder bible and father's name is James, not John.  could not find a Martha, Robert or Elizabeth.  

Found Elizabeth Elder 26 Jan 1864 born Dirraw, Antrim to John Elder and Mary Jane Mccaheron.  This is different DOB than Elder bible, and fathers name John not James, but Dirraw is very small townsland.

Found death of A.  Mary M'Caghern  in Ballymoney,  Antrim in 1871. at age 30 DOB: 1841

Mary jo says she found some info bout during irish potato famine, Elders migrated from island off the coast of Ireland to Antrim.  This could explain why I am not finding other data.

NOT SURE HOW THIS ALL FITS TOGETHER.
Middle name may or may not be Edward:

I CAN NOT FIND ANYTHING DEFINITELY SAYING WHO IS MOTHER IS, although I think Mary Jane McAughin is most likely based upon above finding.  
Menands Albany Rural cemetery listing does not list John Elder parents, nor does his marriage certificate.  

Middle name of "Edward" is uncertain. This could be a different John Elder.

Spouses.Name: Harper-12620
Spouses.DeathLocation: Poughkeepsie, Dutchess, New York, United States
Spouses.bio:
== Biography ==


!900 census states immigration 1888. Immigrated 1890 @ 1930 census. 1920 census says immigrated 1889 and Naturalized 1900.  

Only  real possibility is on ship: FURNESSIA which left from Gasgow, but stopped in Moville and picked up passengers.  Arrived Sept. 4, 1888 It lists her as Mary Jane Harper (She may have taken her mother's first name as her middle name) DOB ~1865.  Traveled alone. 

Likely her route was to take train at Ballyconnell RR (which closed 1890) to Belturbet RR station. Traveled through Clone to Derry, Londonderry where spent night.  Next morning was taken down the Foyle River for about 20 miles, by paddler tenders to Moville where small tenders transported to large  steamships of either Actor or Allen Steamship line.  Not clear to me if these small tenders loaded directly onto the steamship or if they stopped in Moville and transferred from there.  Moville does not appear to have large port, only a small landing. 

1892 census lived in Watervliet with Harper's = Mary (age 26=1866))Jane (age 33=1861)), William (21=18710), Sophia (17=1875)) all born in Ireland.

 Married June 24, 1898 in Jermaine Memorial Presbyterian Church in Watervliet, NY ,  Owned and lived at 128 Third street, Watervliet, NY in 1900-1940.  House valued at $3500 which by today's standards would be about $70,000. 

@to1930 & 1940 census, completed 4th grade and could read and write.

Age 33 when married @ 1930 census

Had very strong Irish brogue.  Her sons told her not to go to their work, because if their bosses heard her brogue, they were afraid they would be fired because of the prejudice against the Irish.

Father was a nailer. Nailers made iron nails which were hand crafted   Mostly used for horseshoes.

She had a stroke.  Grace and John Elder took care of her as long as they could then she was moved to the State Hosp[ital in Poughkeepsie,. NY.  After her death, she was buried Albany Rural Cemetery along with her husband John Elder and son John &Grace Elder in the family plot. Lot 47 Sec 115

NOTE: Based upon funeral records of John Elder DOB 1866  Mary A Haprper, his wife, may have had siblings of : Sophia (Aunt Sophia)[ married George Bohne], Adam, William (as Mrs. William Harper signed the Memorial record).


== Sources ==
<references />
* Albany Rural Cemetery for death date

McCaw-443.Name: McCaw-443
McCaw-443.bio:
[[Category:Derry City Cemetery, Londonderry, County Londonderry]]
[[Category:Presbyterian Ministers]]
== Biography ==

William was born about 1818. 
<ref>Estimated from death 
</ref>

In 1901 William McCaw 80, born Co Londonderry, was living with his daughter and family. Isaac Stevenson 43, biscuit Manufactorer, his wife Florence 36, born Manchester, England, and their children all born Londonderry, Maurice McCaw 11, Irene Constance 8 , Leonard William Hugh 4, Florence Evelyn and 4 servants. <ref> https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1901/Londonderry/Waterside/Victoria_Park/1540882/ </ref> 

In 1861 William 39 from Ireland, a Presbyterian Minister, was living with his wife Sarah 39 from Ireland, and a daughter Mary aged 13, born Manchester in Smedley Lane, Cheetham Hill, Manchester. <ref> "England and Wales Census, 1861", , FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:M7NZ-H8P : Sat Mar 09 18:45:41 UTC 2024), Entry for William McCaw and Sarah McCaw, 1861. </ref> 

William McCaw, widower of Victoria Park, Waterside aged 84, a retired minister died in 1902.Margaret Ferguson of 14 Marlborough Terrace, Londonderry, registered the death. <ref>Londonderry SR District https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/deaths_returns/deaths_1902/05679/4600144.pdf </ref> 
: REV DR. MCCAW.
:The Rev Dr. McCaw formerly Clerk and twice Moderator of the Synod of the English Presbyterian Church, was buried at Londonderry yesterday. The Rev W. M. McPhail, Senior Clerk of the English Synod, conducted the service, and an address was delivered by the Moderator of the General Assembly of the Irish Presbyterian Charch. Representatives of deceased's former church at Manchester attended. <ref> Published: Saturday 03 January 1903 
Newspaper: Daily News (London)  page 3 https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000051/19030103/061/0003 </ref> 

He is buried in Derry City Cemetery, age on headstone 81. <ref>{{FindAGrave| 249336828}}</ref> 
== Sources ==
<references />

Spouses.Name: McGeagh-42
Spouses.bio:
[[Category:Derry City Cemetery, Londonderry, County Londonderry]]
== Biography ==

Sarah was born about 1822 in Cookstown, County Tyrone. She is the daughter of [[McGeagh-14|John McGeagh]].  Her mother may have been Elizabeth McGuin or Elizabeth Rankin.

In 1847 she married Rev. William McCaw, originally from Cookstown but now a Presbyterian minister in Manchester, England<ref>"Ireland Civil Registration Indexes, 1845-1958," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FTB6-VPT : 10 March 2018), MARRIAGES entry for Sarah Mcgeagh; citing Cookstown, 1847, vol. 4, p. 219, General Registry, Custom House, Dublin; FHL microfilm 101,241.</ref> who would go on to be Moderator of the United Presbyterian Synod in 1883.<ref>https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/e9fad747-f86c-4d56-b20a-1df728690a00</ref>  They settled in Manchester where William was a Presbyterian minister.

By 1851 they had two children, Mary and William.<ref>"England and Wales Census, 1851," database with images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:SG16-YZ3 : 11 September 2019), Sarah Mc Caw in household of William Mc Caw, Cheetham, Lancashire, England; citing Cheetham, Lancashire, England, p. 55, from "1851 England, Scotland and Wales census," database and images, findmypast (http://www.findmypast.com : n.d.); citing PRO HO 107, The National Archives of the UK, Kew, Surrey.</ref>  A third, Florence followed in 1862.  By 1871 they were also looking after their 8-year old niece, Sarah Dickson.<ref>"England and Wales Census, 1871", database with images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KDXM-XGB : 10 July 2021), Sarah McCaw in entry for Willm McCaw, 1871.</ref>

In 1861 William 39 from Ireland, a Presbyterian Minister, was living with his wife Sarah 39 from Ireland, and a daughter Mary aged 13, born Manchester, in Smedley Lane, Cheetham Hill, Manchester. <ref> "England and Wales Census, 1861", , FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:M7NZ-H8P : Sat Mar 09 18:45:41 UTC 2024), Entry for William McCaw and Sarah McCaw, 1861. </ref> 

Sarah McCaw of Holly Lodge, died 12th February 1895, married aged 70, wife of a clergyman. Her son in law Isaac Stevenson, of 15 Myrtle Terrace registered the death. <ref>Londonderry SR District https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/deaths_returns/deaths_1895/05941/4687746.pdf (indexed as Sarah McGuran)</ref> She is  buried in Derry Cemetery. <ref>{{FindAGrave| 249336884}} </ref>

44375728.Name: McCaw-454
44375728.bio:
[[Category:Cheltenham Pioneer Cemetery, Cheltenham, Victoria]]
== Biography ==

Thomas was the son of a Weaver, William McCaw and Jane Gilmour of Inch. He was '''christened''' on 17 February 1828 in Wigtownshire. <ref>"Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FMMX-NHV : 16 September 2021), Thomas McCaw, 1828.</ref>

Thomas was employed as a Labourer in Stranraer.

On 6 February 1860, he married Rosanna McHarg at Kirk Road, Stranraer. Thomas was 27 and Rosanna aged 23. Witnesses to their marriage were AM McHarg and A McCaw.<ref>"Scotland Marriages, 1561-1910", , FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XY7G-G7M : 22 December 2023), Rosanna McHarg in entry for Thomas McCaw, 1860.</ref> 

Three months later they sailed on the ''Ocean Home'' from Liverpool to Victoria, Australia. <ref>Public Record Office Victoria; North Melbourne, Victoria; Register of Assisted Immigrants from the United Kindom (refer to microform copy, VPRS 3502); Series: VPRS 14 </ref>They arrived in Australia on 20 August and intended to join Thomas' brother who was living at Northcote.

Known children born in Australia were:
:Margaret (Maggie) McCaw 1861–1908	 
:Jessie McCaw 1863–1868
:Jane McCaw 1864–1936
:Rosanna McCaw 1867–1929	
:Thomas McCaw 1869–1906	
:Elizabeth Ann McCaw 1872–Deceased
:Christina Mary McCaw 1873–1962
:Jessie McCaw 1875–Deceased
:George McCaw 1878–Deceased	
:Euphemia Helena McCaw 1880–1943	
:Violet Helena McCaw 1883–1883	

Thomas was employed with the Victorian Railways.

Thomas McCaw died aged 71 <ref>https://my.rio.bdm.vic.gov.au/efamily-history/66c57a5a9acdab73a7ca3051/record/5c653b384aba80ac318313c2?q=efamily&givenName=Thos&familyName=MCCAW</ref>at Glebe Avenue, Cheltenham.<ref>https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/10339165?searchTerm=MCCAW</ref>  He is buried at Cheltenham Pioneer Cemetery, Cheltenham, Bayside City, Victoria.

Ross-16375.bio:
[[Category:St. John's Church of Ireland Graveyard, Islandmagee, Antrim]]
[[Category:Ballymoney Townland, Island Magee Parish, County Antrim]]
[[Category: Island Magee Parish, County Antrim]]
== Biography ==
Thomas was born on January 7th, 1893 in Ballymoney, Islandmagee, County Antrim, Ireland, the son of [[Ross-16366|Robert Ross]] and [[Ross-16367|Mary Ross]]. His Birth was registered by Maggie Flack of Gransha Islandmagee who was present at the time. <ref>Ireland Civil Registration Birth Index https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/birth_returns/births_1893/02319/1868798.pdf</ref> 

In 1901, Thomas (Age 8) was living in house 1 in Ballymoney, Islandmagee with his parents and 4 of his siblings.<ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1901 Census of Ireland http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1901/Antrim/Islandmagee/Ballymoney/989833/</ref> <ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1901 Census of Ireland Household Return Form http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/reels/nai000359090/</ref>

During the 1911 Census of Ireland, Thomas (Age 18) was still living in Ballymoney, Islandmagee with his parents and brother Robert and sister Catherine.<ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1911 Census of Ireland http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1911/Antrim/Island_Magee/Ballymoney/188214/</ref> <ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1911 Census of Ireland Household Return Form http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/reels/nai001541183/</ref>

Thomas passed away on December 5th, 1955 (Age 62) probably in Islandmagee.<ref>General Register Office (Northern Ireland) D/1955/132/1016/40/14	Thomas	Ross 5th December 1955 62 Years Male	Larne</ref> He is interred in St. John's Church of Ireland Graveyard, in Islandmagee with his Parents and Sister Catherine. <ref>Photo of Gravestone taken by the North of Ireland Family History Society as part of the Islandmagee DNA Group Project 
:''Erected by Robert Ross in memory of his wife Mary Jane Ross, who died 26th July 1928, aged 79 years. Also their son John, killed in action near Arras 28th March 1918, aged 35 years. The above named Robert Ross died 23rd January 1931, aged  81 years. Their son Thomas, died 5th Dec. 1955, aged 62 years. Their daughter Catherine Montgomery, died 20th Jan. 1970, aged 80 years.''</ref>

== Biography == 

Robert was born about 1850, probably in Ballymoney, Islandmagee, County Antrim, Ireland, the son of [[Ross-25891|Andrew Ross]] and [[Unknown-575420|Martha Unknown]].

In 1877 he married [[Ross-16367|Mary Jane Ross]] in Larne Methodist Church, County Antrim. He was a 27 year old mariner living in Ballymoney, Islandmagee and she was 28 years of age living in Gransha, also in Islandmagee. The witnesses were James Ross and Mary Jane Niblock.<ref>Ireland Civil Registration Marriage Index https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1877/11123/8072430.pdf</ref>

In 1901 the couple are living with 5 of their children in Ballymoney and Robert is now a farmer.<ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1901 Ireland Census http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1901/Antrim/Islandmagee/Ballymoney/989833/</ref> In 1911 they are still living in Ballymoney with 3 of their children. All 7 of their children are still alive.<ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1911 Ireland Census http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1911/Antrim/Island_Magee/Ballymoney/188214/</ref>

He passed away in 1931, probably in Ballymoney, Islandmagee.<ref>General Register Office (Northern Ireland) D/1931/129/1016/11/220 Robert	Ross 23rd January 1931	81 Years Male Larne</ref> He is interred in St. John's Church of Ireland Graveyard, in Islandmagee with his wife, and two of their "children".<ref>Photo of Gravestone taken by the North of Ireland Family History Society as part of the Islandmagee DNA Group Project 
:''Erected by Robert Ross in memory of his wife Mary Jane Ross, who died 26th July 1928, aged 79 years. Also their son John, killed in action near Arras 28th March 1918, aged 35 years. The above named Robert Ross died 23rd January 1931, aged  81 years. Their son Thomas, died 5th Dec. 1955, aged 62 years. Their daughter Catherine Montgomery, died 20th Jan. 1970, aged 80 years.''</ref>

== Biography == 

Mary was born in 1848 in Gransha, Islandmagee, County Antrim, Ireland, the daughter of [[Ross-26189|James Ross]]. a cooper, and [[Dick-4754|Catherine Dick]]. She was baptised on 12-Nov-1848 in Islandmagee Methodist Church.<ref>Islandmagee Methodist Church Baptisms 1830-1917. Transcribed by the North of Ireland Family History Society www.nifhs.org.</ref>

In 1877 she married [[Ross-16366|Robert Ross]] in Larne Methodist Church, County Antrim. He was a 27 year old mariner living in Ballymoney, Islandmagee and she was 28 years of age living in Gransha, also in Islandmagee. The witnesses were [[Ross-16368|James Ross]] and Mary Jane Niblock.<ref>Ireland Civil Registration Marriage Index https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1877/11123/8072430.pdf</ref>

All 7 of their children are still alive.<ref>1911 Ireland Census http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1911/Antrim/Island_Magee/Ballymoney/188214/</ref>

Mary Jane passed away on July 24th, 1928, probably in Ballymoney, Islandmagee. Note that Mary Jane's Gravestone records her passing as 26th July. <ref>General Register Office (Northern Ireland) D/1928/129/1016/11/65 Mary Ross 24th July 1928 79 Years Female Larne </ref> She is interred in St. John's Church of Ireland Graveyard, Islandmagee.<ref>Photo of Gravestone taken by the North of Ireland Family History Society as part of the Islandmagee DNA Group Project

== Biography ==
Thomas was born in 1863, probably in Gransha, Islandmagee, County Antrim, Ireland, the son of [[Ross-26224|James Ross]] and [[Dick-4754|Catherine Dick]]. He was baptised on 06-Nov-1863 in Islandmagee Methodist Church.

In 1891, Thomas married [[Ross-25889|Ann Jane ("Annie") Ross]] at the 1st Presbyterian Church in Larne, County Antrim. He was recorded as full age, a Bachelor and a farmer residing in Gransha, Islandmagee. Annie was recorded as full age, and a spinster residing in Walbrook Cottage, Islandmagee. Unfortunately their Father's names were reversed on their marriage record. Thomas' Father was James Ross (Farmer) and Annie's Father was John Ross (Mariner)<ref>Ireland Civil Registration Marriage Index https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1891/10666/5886623.pdf</ref>

During the 1901 Census of Ireland, Thomas and Annie were residing in a house 32 in Gransha (Islandmagee, Antrim) with their 4 sons.<ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1901 Census of Ireland http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1901/Antrim/Islandmagee/Gransha/990088/</ref><ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1901 Census of Ireland Household Return Form http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/reels/nai000359403/</ref>

:Ross	John Alex 7	Male	Son	Methodist	Co Antrim
:Ross	Thomas	5	Male	Son	Methodist	Co Antrim
:Ross	William	2	Male	Son	Methodist	Co Antrim

Thomas and Annie were residing in a house 4 in Gransha (Island Magee, Antrim) during the 1911 Census of Ireland, with their 4 sons still residing with them. It was recorded they had 4 total children with 4 still living at the time of the census.<ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1911 Census of Ireland http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1911/Antrim/Island_Magee/Gransha/188422/</ref><ref>The National Archives of Ireland 1911 Census of Ireland Household Return Form http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/reels/nai001541743/</ref>

Thomas passed away on November 14th, 1938 (age 75).<ref>General Register Office (Northern Ireland) D/1938/129/1016/12/148 Thomas Ross 14th November 1938 75 Years Male Larne</ref> He is interred in St. John's Church of Ireland Graveyard, in Islandmagee.<ref>Photo of Gravestone in St. John's Church of Ireland Graveyard, in Islandmagee, taken by the North of Ireland Family History Society as part of the Islandmagee DNA Group Project.
: ''In loving memory of Thomas Ross who died at Calgary 13th January 1935 aged 38 years. And his sister Annie who died 20th October 1935 aged 23 years. Also their Father Thomas Ross who died 14th November 1938 aged 75 years. And their Mother Ann Jane died 14th April 1949 aged 80 years''.</ref> He left a will, and probate was granted to his widow Ann Ross.<ref>Public Record Office of Northern Ireland Will Calendars https://apps.proni.gov.uk/WillsCalendar_IE/WillsSearch.aspx [no image of will available] Ross Thomas of Gransha Islandmagee county Antrim farmer died 14 November 1938 Probate Belfast 25 November to Ann Jane Ross the widow. Effects £294 15s</ref>

== Biography == 
James was born about 1813,<ref>Estimated from age at death.</ref> probably in Islandmagee, County Antrim, Ireland..

He was a cooper and a farmer and married to [[Dick-4754|Catherine Dick]].

James passed away in Gransha, Islandmagee, County Antrim 18 May 1891 from decay of nature, aged 78 years. He was married and a farmer. The death was registered by his daughter [[Ross-26190|Margaret Flack]] of Gransha who was present at his death.<ref>Ireland Civil Registration Death Index https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/deaths_returns/deaths_1891/06075/4732431.pdf </ref>  He is interred in St. John's Church of Ireland Graveyard, Islandmagee.<ref>Gravestone Inscriptions, County Antrim, Volume 1, Islandmagee. Compiled by George Rutherford (1977).
:''Erected by James Ross in memory of his son Thomas who departed this life 2nd August 1862 aged 22 years. The above-named James Ross died 18th May 1891 aged 78 years. Also his wife Catherine DICK, who died 24th Sepr 1892 aged 71 years. Also their son Alexander aged 31 years, and his wife Maggie JOHNSTON aged 31 years, who were drowned by the foundering of the Barque "Alice M. Craig", 9th March 1893.'' </ref>

Stewart-50419.Name: Stewart-50419
Stewart-50419.bio:
{{Estimated Date}}
[[Category: Kilrea Village, County Londonderry]]
== Biography ==
: ''— Please see research note, below, re Stewart family name. —''

: Margaret McKay (family name unknown) was born about 1784.<ref name="death-notice">''Londonderry Standard'', 11 March 1858 (pg. 2). Death notice: "March 2, Margaret, relict of the late Mr. Wm. M'Kay, of Church-street, Kilrea, in the 75th year of her age." Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-06-09).</ref>

: Margaret and her husband, [[McKay-8570|William]], lived in Church-street in Kilrea.<ref name="death-notice" />

: When the 1831 census was enumerated for Ireland, Margaret's household comprised one family of five males and five females. Nine adhered to the Church of Ireland, and the tenth was Presbyterian.<ref>''Ireland 1831 Census''. County of Londonderry, Parish of Kilrea, Barony of Loughinsholin. Digital images hosted online by the National Archives of Ireland (Dublin), censusnationalarchives.ie. Extract by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-06-08).</ref>

: In 1849, Margaret's grandson, [[McKay-8687|Thomas]], emigrated to Adelaide, Australia. By 1857, his family had lost touch with him, as evidenced from the following notice reprinted from the ''Missing Friends and Australian Advertiser'' in June 1857:
:: ''   560. McKay, Thomas, aged 28, of Kilrea, County Londonderry, Ireland, Solciitor; left London for Adelaide, in 1849, in the Royal Sovereign, never heard from; is supposed to have gone to sea soon after his arrival at Adelaide.—Come home or write to your father immediately, or to Dr. McKay, 38, George-street, North, Sydney; if in difficulties your father will relieve you at once. Any party who may be instrumental in bringing this inquiry under the notice of the said Thomas McKay shall be liberally rewarded, and in case of death £5 reward will be paid for a well authenticated certificate of the fact, on application to Mr. S. Curtis, 20, Finsbury-street, London''.  <ref name="derry-journal-1857">''Derry Journal'', 3 June 1857 (pg. 4). "Missing Friends." Citing Thomas McKay, age 28, formerly of Kilrea, who emigrated to Adelaide, Australia; citing also Dr. [Charles] McKay of Sydney. Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-05-10).</ref> It is not yet known whether the McKay family of Kilrea re-established contact with Thomas. ~[[Kilpatrick-1128]] (2022-07-13)

: Immediately preceding this notice, was printed the following:
::''   559. Stewart, William, aged 40, Land Surveyor, native of Kilrea, Londonderry, Ireland; left for Adelaide in 1849. Was in Melbourne in 1849, when he sent a newspaper to his brother, since when he has not been heard of by his friends in Ireland. A considerable sum of money has been left you by your uncle Charles. Write to Mrs. McKay, Church-street, Kilrea, Ireland, or to Dr. McKay, 38, George-street, north, Sydney. In case of death a liberal reward will be given for a well authenticated certificate, addressed to the above Dr. McKay, by whom also any information will be thankfully received''. <ref name="derry-journal-1857" />

:: William Stewart's uncle Charles was probably the same whose death was noticed in the ''Coleraine Chronicle'' several years earlier:
::''   In Kilrea, on Wednesday morning, the 11th inst., [[Stewart-50420|Mr. Charles Stewart]], land-surveyor, in the 73rd year of his age''. <ref name="death-charles-stewart">''Coleraine Chronicle'', 21 June 1851 (pg. 2). Death notice for Charles Stewart of Kilrea, aged 72 years. Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-07-13).</ref>

: On 2nd March 1858, Margaret McKay died in Kilrea, aged seventy-four years.<ref name="death-notice" />

== Research notes ==
* ''Family surname, Stewart?'' — Mrs. Margaret McKay was a contemporary of Charles Stewart who died at Kilrea in 1851, aged seventy-two years.<ref name="death-charles-stewart" /> She was the contact person for Mr. Stewart's nephew, William in Adelaide, Australia, with respect to a legacy left by Charles to William,<ref name="derry-journal-1857" /> suggesting that Mrs. McKay had a very close connection to the Stewarts. Because a suggestion or inference does not provide substantive evidence, the Stewart surname is advanced tentatively. 
:: ''— Evidence which either corroborates or disproves this assertion would be most welcome. — '' [[Kilpatrick-1128]] (2022-07-13)
* The year of birth, c.1784, was approximated from the age recorded at death.<ref name="death-notice" /> Given that Margaret's son, [[McKay-8670|Marshall]], was born c.1798, Margaret's year of birth was probably earlier than 1784 and/or Marshall's somewhat later than 1798. ~[[Kilpatrick-1128]] (2022-07-13)
* Margaret was cited as the mother of [[McKay-8629|Charles McKay]] who emigrated to Sydney, Australia and died there in 1898.<ref>New South Wales, Australia. [https://familyhistory.bdm.nsw.gov.au/ Family History Search]. Index entry: Charles McKay died in Petersham district in 1898, father: not stated, mother: Margaret, registration no. 2987/1898 (accessed 2022-06-08).</ref>
* This profile is part of a longer-term project, conducted by [[Kilpatrick-1128]], to catalogue the various McKay families in the parishes of Kilrea and Tamlaght O'Crilly, county Londonderry. (2022-06-09)

== Biography ==
: Marshall McKay was born about 1798,<ref name="death-notice-1">''Belfast News-Letter'', 30 October 1860 (pg. 2). Death notice: "October 27, Marshall M'Kay, Esq., merchant, Kilrea, aged 62 years." Digital image online at ancestry.ca; transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-05-06.</ref> <ref name="death-notice-2">''The Herald'' (Melbourne, Victoria, Australia), 7 February 1861 (pg. 4). Death notice: "On the 27th October last, of apoplexy, at Kilrea, Ireland, Marshall McKay, Esq. aged 62 years, father of Mr. Thomas McKay, solicitor." Digital image online at Trove, trove.nla.gov.au. Transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-05-06.</ref> probably in the town or parish of Kilrea where his parents,  [[McKay-8570|William McKay]] and [[Unknown-606855|Margaret]], his wife, held land.

: Mr. McKay was a shopkeeper and merchant by trade, operating his business out of The Diamond in Kilrea.<ref name="zettam" /> He also traded as a woollen draper and spirit & porter dealer.<ref>Isaac Slater's ''Commercial Directory of Ireland'' (1846). Digital images online at FindMyPast.co.uk (accessed 2022-05-09).</ref>

: Marshall's wife was [[Crawford-23405|Mary Ann Crawford]], daughter of James Crawford of Carmagrim townland, near Portglenone, in county Antrim.<ref name="zettam">Church of Ireland. Parish Church of Kilrea, county Londonderry. ''Transcripts of baptisms 1829-61, marriages 1829-48, and burials 1829-62  by Zara Mettam, 1967''. Copy on FHL film no. 908817; online at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/ FamilySearch Int'l.] (accessed 2022-05-28).</ref> <ref>O'Keeffe, Pauline, Barbara Braswell, Derek Torrens ''et al'', compilers. Kilrea Parish Church Records [St. Patrick's, Church of Ireland]. Transcripts hosted online at [http://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/index.html Bann Valley Genealogy] by Richard Torrens (accessed 2022-05-28).</ref> <ref>''Londonderry Sentinel'', 11 March 1843 (pg. 3). Death notice: "On Tuesday, the 28th ult., at the house of her son-in-law, Marshall M'Kay, Esq., of Kilrea, in the 83d year of her age, Mrs. Crawford, relict of [the] late Mr. James Crawford, of Carnniegrim [Carmagrim], near Portglenone, and sister of the late Dr. John Hamilton, of the Hon. the East India Company's service." Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-07-19).</ref>

: After a life preoccupied with the nature of trade, and in service to his community (see transcripts of contemporary news articles, below), Marshall McKay, Esq., died at Kilrea on 27th October 1860. He was in his sixty-third year. The newspapers noticed his death, both at home in Ireland and abroad, in Australia, still seeking information of the deceased Mr. Marshall's son, Thomas. <ref name="death-notice-1" />
:: ''On the 27th October last, of apoplexy, at Kilrea, Ireland, Marshall McKay, Esq. aged 62 years, father of Mr. Thomas McKay, solicitor.'' — ''The Herald'' (Melbourne, Australia), 7 February 1861. <ref name="death-notice-2" />

: Mr. McKay's body was buried in the churchyard of St. Patrick (Church of Ireland) in Kilrea.<ref name="zettam" /> <ref>Braswell, Barbara, compiler. ''Kilrea Parish Church: St. Patrick's – Burial Register, 1829–1863''. Transcripts made in 2008. Hosted online by Richard Torrens at [http://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/index.html Bann Valley Genealogy] (accessed 2022-05-28).</ref> His estate was administered by his son, James McKay of Kilrea.<ref>Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (Belfast). ''Will Calendars''. Index entry: "Marshall McKay, registry: Londonderry, date of death: 27th October 1860; date of grant: 4th February 1861; effects under £5000; abstract: Letters of Administration of the personal estate of Marshall MKay late of Kilrea in the County of Londonderry Merchant deceased who died 27 October 1860 at same place were granted at Londonderry to James M'Kay of Kilrea aforesaid Merchant the Son one of the next of kin of said deceased." Index entry and digital image online at apps.proni.gov.uk (extract by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-06-09).</ref>

=== Descendants ===

: Marshall and Mary Ann McKay had several children, several of whom died in childhood or young adulthood. The 1831 census of Ireland enumerated their household under the name, Marshall McCay, in the town of Kilrea. The family then consisted of three males [Marshall and sons, Thomas and James] and three females [wife, Mary Ann or Marian, and two other females, perhaps daughters]. The family professed the Church of Ireland as their religious denomination.<ref>[http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie Ireland 1831 Census]. Household of Marshall McCay, no. 193, in the town and parish of Kilrea, barony of Loughinsholin, and county of Londonderry. Digital image hosted online (accessed 2022-05-06).</ref>  — Note: Text appearing [within square brackets] represents editorial remarks by the compiler. ~[[Kilpatrick-1128]] 

: Five of their children died as children or young adults:
* their eldest daughter, [[McKay-8722|Nancy]], who died of consumption in 1846, aged eleven years;
* [[McKay-8718|William]], who died of pulmonary consumption in 1848, aged fifteen years;
* [[McKay-8719|Margaret]], who died in 1850, aged twelve years;
* [[McKay-8720|Marshall, jun.]], who died in January, 1860 (nine months before his father's death), aged twenty years; and
* [[McKay-8721|Sarah]], who died of "decline," in November, 1860 (one month before the death of her father), aged eighteen years.

: Their second eldest, [[McKay-8696|James]], died two years after he married. He was afflicted wtih kidney disease, and died in 1864, aged thirty-four years. His daughter, [[McKay-8697|Margaret Ann]], bore two children: [[McElfatrick-23|John Ernest McElfatrick]], who died in 1917, aged twenty-four years and unmarried; and, [[McElfatrick-22|Eileen Sarah Templeton McElfatrick]], who lived into old age, and died in 1963, unmarried.

: Marshall's eldest son, Thomas, left for Australia and appears never to have been heard from again, as reported in the ''Derry Journal'' on 3rd June 1857:
:: ''Missing Friends''.
:: ''   We (Coleraine Chronicle) have received a copy of a London monthly newspaper entitled the Missing Friends and Australian Advertiser, ...'' 
:: ''   "560. McKay, Thomas, aged 28, of Kilrea, County Londonderry, Ireland, Solciitor; left London for Adelaide, in 1849, in the Royal Sovereign, never heard from; is supposed to have gone to sea soon after his arrival at Adelaide.—Come home or write to your father immediately, or to [[McKay-8629|Dr. McKay]], 38, George-street, North, Sydney; if in difficulties your father will relieve you at once. Any party who may be instrumental in bringing this inquiry under the notice of the said Thomas McKay shall be liberally rewarded, and in case of death £5 reward will be paid for a well authenticated certificate of the fact, on application to Mr. S. Curtis, 20, Finsbury-street, London."''  <ref>''Derry Journal'', 3 June 1857 (pg. 4). "Missing Friends." Citing Thomas McKay, age 28, formerly of Kilrea, who emigrated to Adelaide, Australia. Digital image online at findmypast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-05-06.</ref>

: It would appear, then, that this line became extinct, unless Thomas can be found in the historical records and to have had a family.

=== The Diamond, Kilrea (OS ref. 3) ===
: This parcel comprised a house, office, and yard, rented by Marshall McKay and his descendants to various tenants over the years. As suggested by the name, Situated in the heart of the town, at the confluence of Coleraine, Maghera, Church, and Bridge Streets, occupants of the The Diamond included the Mercers' Company agent's office and, for the most part, other shopkeepers.

=== Notes re: lands held ===
* All land area stated in terms of English statute measure.
* All holdings were let by the Mercers Company of London, unless the parcel was sub-let to a sub-tenant by the lessee.
* Griffith's = Griffith's Valuation, completed in the parish of Kilrea on 6th October 1858.
* VRB = Valuation Revision Book, of which there are several. These Valuation Revision Books detail the changes in tenancy and the holding itself from 1864–1929.
* Land holdings often extended past the date of death, pending administration of an estate.

=== Public dinner in Kilrea, 1838 ===
: ''Londonderry Standard'', 19th September 1838: <ref name="transcript-1838">''Londonderry Standard'', 19 September 1838 (pg. 2). "Public Dinner in Kilrea." Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-07-17).</ref>
: ''   Public Dinner in Kilrea''.
: ''   On Thursday, the 6th instant, the shareholders of the Kilrea Union Conveyance Company, dined together in the Town-hall of Kilrea. The room was well lighted up, and tastefully festooned with laurels, evergreens, flowers, &c., under the immediate direction of Mr. Chambers, architect, who deserves great credit for the superior taste and abilities displayed in superintending the various decorations. Immediately over the chairman, was a striking and well executed likeness of our youthful and beloved Queen; and, at the opposite end of the room, was a drawing of the harp, surmounted by the crown. The rose, shamrock, and thistle (enclosed in a wreath of evergreens,) were placed in different parts of the chamber. About fifty gentlemen sat down to dinner—Wm. H. Holmes,† Esq., J.P., officiated as chairman with great judgment and ability. The Rev. Mr. Wallace acted as vice-president. Dinner was laid on the table at half-past six o'clock, and served up by Mr. Adcock, of the Mercers' Hotel, in his usual splendid style. There was an ample profusion of dishes, viands, sweetmeats, &c. including all the delicacies of the season. After the cloth was removed, several loyal and patriotic toasts were drunk. The first toast on the list was''
: ''   The Queen''.
: ''   The chairman on rising to propose it, took occasion to observe that, although her Majesty was young, he hoped she would be able, from the support of a loyal and obedient people, to discharge the functions of government with vigour and ability. The toast was received with every demonstration of loyalty''.
: ''   The Queen Dowager and the rest of the Royal Family''.
: ''   Lord Hill and the Army''.
: ''   The Navy''.
: ''   Joseph Clarke, Esq., M.D., R.N., returned thanks in appropriate terms''.
: ''   The chairman on proposing the next toast observed that although an Englishman, he and his family were now intimately connected with Ireland and its welfare, and that he never had greater pleasure in his life than being called on to preside where there were so many Irish faces beaming with delight before him. He would now give''
: ''   The Lord Lieutenant and the prosperity of their native land, Drank with all the honours—"Patrick's Day."''
: ''   Success to the Union Conveyance. Nine times nine''.
: ''   Mr. J.G. Simpson returned thanks''.
: ''   The Town and Trade of Kilrea. Six times six—"Life let us cherish."''
: ''   '''Mr. Marshall M'Kay''' briefly returned thanks''.
: ''   The Linen Trade and prosperity to it''.
: ''   Mr. William M'Kay, in returning thanks, stated that the Linen Trade was now in a more flourishing condition than it had been for some time past—an observation which was received with loud cheers''.
: ''   The Agricultural Interest. "Speed the Plough."''
: ''   Mr. M'Cleery eloquently returned thanks''.
: ''   The Town and Trade of Belfast. Received with great enthusiasm—"Donegall March."''
: ''   Mr. Daniel Ferris returned thanks in a very animated style, and alluded in glowing terms to the prosperous state of trade in Belfast—its rising importance in the commercial world—the industry, perseverance, and enterprise of the merchants, and the intimate connection of the traders of Kilrea with them in mercantile affairs. Its charitable institutions and public seminaries were highly eulogised in very eloquent terms. His speech was received throughout with much applause''.
: ''   The City and Trade of Londonderry. "First of August."''
: ''   Dr. Hunter returned thanks, and stated how he, as one of a deputation from the Union Company to Londonderry was warmly received by the inhabitants of that place, and the interest they felt in a conveyance being started between Belfast and their City; and, on the whole, that he never was better pleased in his life than with the frankness and cordiality displayed towards him and his colleagues on their recent visit to that ancient City, and that such a promise as the interest and support of a majority of the respectable and independent inhabitants of Londonderry was surely the strongest link in the union chain''.
: ''   The Shareholders of the Union Conveyance Company. Nine times nine—tremendous cheering—"Sae will we yet."''
: ''   Surgeon Church begged the indulgence of the chair and the assembly, while he said a few words with regard to the Union Company, the causes of its formation, and the motives whereby it was actuated. First, with regard to the Union Company, its members were unanimously determined that it should not belie its name, that it should be a Union Company not only in name but in reality, and that no private jobbing should be allowed to take share in its transactions; and that, no matter how the shareholders differed in opinion, they possessed perfect unanimity in one thing, namely, an earnest desire to do all in their power that would be conducive to the comfort and accommodation of persons travelling by their conveyance, as well as advantageous to the interests of the shareholders themselves; and he said that this consideration caused him to allude to the reasons why the Union Company had been formed, that it was because they believed there would no longer be any direct travelling, by Kilrea, between Londonderry and Belfast, unless they started a conveyance themselves. After a few other brief remarks, he concluded by thanking the meeting for the patience with which they had been pleased to hear him, as likewise for the honour conferred on him in being called on to respond to the toast, which had been so enthusiastically drunk''.
: ''   The non-shareholders who have honoured us with their presence—"Come a' the gither."''
: ''   The Rev. Mr. M'Cammon eloquently returned thanks''.
: ''   The chairman at this time was about to retire, when the Vice-President briefly proposed his health. After having returned thanks in an eloquent and animated speech he withdrew, when Mr. Turnbull was elected in his place. Shortly after which the Vice President gave''
: ''   The health of, and long life to Mrs. Holmes, the benefactress of the poor—"Jessie the flower of Dumblane." This toast was enthusiastically received.''
: ''   Dr. Clarke briefly returned thanks''.
: ''   Many other toasts were given and replied to by the Rev. Mr. Wallace, Mr. O'Neill, Mr. Brown, Mr. Chambers, Mr. Bradley, Mr. Kane, &c. At intervals the band played some appropriate and beautiful airs. The conviviality of the meeting was kept up until a late hour with great spirit; their hilarity was unceasingly displayed throughout the night, and each person, on retiring, seemed highly delighted with the festivities of the evening''.  <ref name="transcript-1838" />

=== Address to W.H. Holmes, 1843 ===
: ''Banner of Ulster'', 28th April 1843: <ref>''Banner of Ulster'', 28 April 1843 (pg. 3). "Address and Presentation to W.H. Holmes, Esq." Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-07-17).</ref>

=== Presbyterian movement, 1844 ===
: ''Dublin Evening Post'', 4th April 1844: <ref name="presbyterian-1844">''Dublin Evening Post'', 4 April 1844 (pg. 4). "Presbyterian Movement. ... Kilrea." Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-07-17).</ref>
: ''   Presbyterian Movement. ... Kilrea''.
: ''A meeting was held here on the 26th ult. Notwithstanding the urgent claims of husbandry at this season of the year, and though the meeting was announced for twelve o'clock, noon, yet long before that hour vast numbers had assembled at the First Presbyterian Church, while the peals of its fine deep-toned bell swept over the adjoining district; and if the Primate, with his friends, could have witnessed the determined appearance of the crowds collected there, they must have felt that they have precipitated a crisis which may be fatal to mitres and Apostolic succession-despotism in Ulster and elsewhere. The Minister of the First Presbyterian Church, after prayer, proposed as chairman a person who resided among them, and who was not the less respected because he was a member of the Irish Established Church, attached to its evangelical truth, and actuated by liberal Christian feelings. He proposed that '''Marshall M'Kay, of Kilrea, Esq.''', do take the chair, which was carried by acclamation.—On taking the chair, Mr. M'Kay said that he was a member of the Established Church; but yet, he felt that the treatment Presbyterians had received in the affair of mixed marriages was most insulting and unjust. No course could be taken in Ireland more dangerous and ungrateful than that adopted towards them. He fully concurred with them in seeking equal rights. The Rev. Mr. Rogers [sic] rose, and said that he was not surprised to see, on that occasion, the larged and most respectable meeting every assembled on any former occasion in Kilrea. It was the meeting, not of a faction, but of a deeply-injured people, to remonstrate, to petition for redress, to crave public support; and there were present, as their friends and advocates, many members of every religious denomination around them. He would not despair of final success; but be the period of final trial long or short, the friends of truth had but one course open to them. In the meantime, of Scriptural rights they must abandon no privilege and quail before no enemy. The Rev. Mr. Denham, of Boveedy, proposed a number of excellent resolutions, and, in recommending their adoption, defended the Scriptural foundation of the Presbyterian Church and ministry, and took occasion to contrast it with the arrogant and unscriptural claims of Puseyite prelacy. His speech was warmly responded to, and to produce a great sensation. The Rev. Dr. Brown seconded the resolutions in a most effective speech. He briefly adverted to the attempted spoliation of Presbyterianism throughout the British empire, and the bold but unsuccessful effort made last year to prostrate the liberties of England beneath the feet of an intolerant faction—a faction which grasped at universal spiritual despotism, and but recently indoctrinated the King of Prussia in Britain's Royal and Apostolical palaces, and charged him on to a mad but vain crusade against the religious liberties of his subjects. The spirit of the age was uniting the evangelical members of all denominations against their common and deadly foe. That spirit hailed from the Socinian Robberty Protection Bill of Lyndhurst, and passed the Aristocratic Gamblers' Indemnity Bill, and ruthlessly destroyed the Established Church of Scotland, and drove forth its faithful ministers and people from their homes and the houses where they worshipped God, and refused them  beild or shelter from rain or storm, save the canopy of heaven, or the bosom of the deep sea. Great principles were being taught. The empire must know that Scripture truth is in deadly peril. Silent endurance is no longer a duty, and a spirit has been evoked, which, in all probability, shall speedily test all the religious principles of the empire. Already, too, as if stricken with prudent fear, when, as of old, the oppressed servants of God should resuscitate the Solemn League and Covenant, and append their names, and stand by each other in maintaining its engagements. The rev. doctor's speech was received with great cheering. The Rev. Mr. Wallace made some very happy and impressive observations. The Rev. Andrew Todd next addressed the meeting, and, in a brief and remarkably lucid speech, reviewed the course adopted towards Presbyterians on the question of mixed marriages. The Rev. Wm. Kennedy M'Kay then addressed the meeting. This great meeting was terminated by the usual vote to the chairman and the Apostolical benediction, between five and six o'clock. The petitions were most numerously signed''.  <ref name="presbyterian-1844" />

=== Dublin, Belfast, & Coleraine Railway, 1845 ===

=== Kilrea relief committee, 1847 ===
: ''Coleraine Chronicle'', 29th May 1847: <ref name="kilrea-relief">''Coleraine Chronicle'', 29 May 1847 (pg. 3). "Kilrea." (relief committee.) Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-07-17).</ref>
: ''   Kilrea.—A relief committee was formed at Kilrea, in December last, called the Kilrea District Committee, and from a fund raised by voluntary subscriptions from the Mercers' Company, gentlemen, clergy, the shopkeepers of Kilrea, and the farmers of the district, 230 families were relieved two days in the week with soup and meal, for the most part gratis, to the 26th of April, when a committee was appointed under the out-door relief act, consisting of the following gentlemen:—George Bicknell, Esq., chairman; Rev. Thomas Lindsay; Rev. H.W. Rodgers, Rev. Samuel Otterson, '''Mr. M. M'Kay''', Mr. Thomas M'Cotter, guardians; and Mr. Wm. Adcock, Kilrea, Mr. John Kennedy, jun., Tamlaght, and Mr. Henry O'Neal, Kilrea, ratepayers. The destitute and those out of employment are supplied with food gratis, and those employed at cost price. There has been no rate struck as yet on the Kilrea division, nor will it be for some time to come, as government gave an equal sum to that subscribed; the remainder was handed over to the finance committee at Ballymoney, which will supply the committee for a length of time. Too much praise cannot be given to George Bicknell, Esq., Charles Bicknell, Esq., and Miss Bicknell, for their indefatigable exertions in behalf of the poor, by giving meal, rice, and money from their own private purses, and by sending a daily supply of food to one hundred children in the male and female schools at Movanagher. Mr. Bicknell also distributed two tons of meal weekly, by order of the Company, to the poorer tenantry and cottiers; at first it was given at half-price, and afterwards gratuitously, but has been discontinued, unless in cases of fever or sickness, since the relief act came into operation.—Communicated''.  <ref name="kilrea-relief" />

=== Tenants of the Mercers' Company, 1849 ===
: ''Coleraine Chronicle'', 23rd June 1849:  <ref name="irish-tenantry-1849">''Coleraine Chronicle'', 23 June 1849 (pg. 2). "The Irish Tenantry of the Mercers' Company" at Kilrea. Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-07-17).</ref>
: ''   The Irish Tenantry of the Mercers' Company.—At a meeting of the tenantry of the Worshipful the Mercers' Company, held on the 14th inst., at Kilrea, '''Mr. Marshall M'Kay''' in the chair, a petition was drawn up to that respected body, praying an abatement of rent, suited to the altered circumstances of the petitioners. The memorialists express in their petition their unabated confidence in the generosity and sense of justice of the Worshipful Company, dwelt upon their losses and privations, occasioned by successive failures of the potato crop, the present ruinous price of flax and butter—almost the only articles by which they had, in former years, the means of paying their rents—and inability, even with the greatest self-denial and self-sacrifice, to eke out the sum needed for their present rent, which was fixed in 1834, when the quantity of the produce of their farms was much more considerable than now, and for present taxes, which had added an unexpected addition to their rents of about ten per cent. The memorial is an able, well-written statement of facts, to which, we trust, the influential and considerate Mercers' Company will respond in a manner worthy of their character as a corporate body, and with a due regard to the interests of tenants who have struggled arduously and perseveringly to meet their just obligations. At the meeting the following resolution was unanimously adopted—a resolution alike creditable to the tenantry, to the Mercers' Company, and to Mr. Bicknell the respected and worthy agent of the Company. "Resolved—That in holding the present meeting, to solicit our landlords to grant us a reduction of rents, we hereby declare ourselves impelled by our worldly difficulties alone to do so, and that we avail ourselves of the present occasion to express our continued respect and confidence in the Worshipful the Mercers' Company, London, and in George Bicknell, Esq., their Irish agent, whose conduct in all respects has been such as to merit our high approbation."''  <ref name="irish-tenantry-1849" />

== Biography ==
{{Ireland Native}}
: William McKay, jun., was born about 1803, probably at or near the town of Kilrea in county Derry.<ref name="death-notice">''Belfast News-Letter, 10 December 1860'' (pg. 2). Death notice: "December 6, at Kilrea, Mr. William M'Kay, aged 56 years." Digital image online at ancestry.ca; transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-05-06.</ref> He was the son of [[McKay-8570|William McKay, sen.]] and [[Unknown-606855|Margaret]], his wife.<ref>Griffith's Valuation (1858) and the Valuation Revision Books (1864–1901), together with the death notice (1858) for William McKay, jun.'s [[Unknown-606855|mother]], show that this McKay family was the only McKay household domiciled in Church-street in Kilrea from the early to late 1800s. The valuation records are shown in this profile for William McKay, jun.(months after the death of his mother), and for his siblings, John and Elizabeth.</ref>

: A few months after his mother's death, William's name was entered into Griffith's Valuation as the head of the household in Church-street in the town of Kilrea. Precisely where on Church-street this tenement stood is not known. However, it was enumerated close to the record entries for Kilrea Presbyterian church, St. Patrick's church, and the rectory. William also held three rural leaseholds:
* 9 acres 1 rood 30 perches of land in Kilrea townland (OS ref. 16), a parcel which lay up the Garvagh road about 1/4 mile northeast of the town;
* 7 acres 0 roods 25 perches of land in Claragh townland (OS ref. 41), a field which lay in the southeastern portion of the townland, and a half mile or so from the town of Kilrea; and,
* 7 acres 0 roods 15 perches, also in Claragh, a field which lay just west of the parcel cited above.<ref name="griffith">Griffith, Richard. ''General Valuation of Rateable Property in Ireland. == Lands held ==

=== Church-street, Kilrea (OS ref. 25) ===
: This parcel comprised a house, offices, yard and garden on 21 perches of land, apparently near the parish church of St. Patrick. It was held as follows:
: – 1858-10-06: landholder: William M'Kay [jun.] (source: Griffith's) <ref name="griffiths-william">Griffith, Richard. ''General Valuation of Rateable Property in Ireland''. "Union of Ballymoney (Part of). Valuation of the Several Tenements comprising that portion of the above-named Union situate in the County of Londonderry." Extracts for the land holdings of William McKay, jun. (c.1803–1860) in the town of Kilrea and in Claragh townland, in the parish of Kilrea, 6th October 1858. Dublin: Alex. Thom and Sons, 1858. Digital images of tables and maps online at AskAboutIreland.ie (extracts by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-06-10).</ref> 
: – 1864–1868: John McKay [brother of William, jun.] (source: 1st VRB, and so on)
: – 1868–1899: Elizabeth McKay. In 1880, her brother, John, returned to the house on Church-street as an occupier.
: – 1899–1910: James Stenson [var. Stinson], a nephew to Elizabeth. James died in 1910.
: – 1911: The house went out of the McKay family's hands to a Mark Reilly. <ref name="vrb" /> —Note: This OS ref. (25) was merged with the house at OS ref. 24, and James Stinson's widow continued to live in Church-street until her death in 1928.

=== Kilrea townland (OS ref. 16) ===
: This parcel lay in open countryside, lying up the Garvagh road about 1/4 mile NE of the town of Kilrea. It comprised  9 acres 1 rood 30 perches and was held as follows:
: – 1858-10-06: landholder: William M'Kay [jun.] (source: Griffith's) <ref name="griffiths-william" />
: – 1864–1866: John McKay.
: – 1866–1867: James Shields (apparently a sub-let. ~[[Kilpatrick-1128]] 2022-07-03.)
: – 1867–1901: Elizabeth McKay. In 1879, the size of the parcel was reduced to 9 acres 15 perches.
: – 1901: James Stinson purchased the parcel in fee.
: – 1901–1918: James Stinson.
: – 1918–1929: Rachel Stinson [widow of James]. <ref name="vrb" />

=== Claragh townland (OS ref. 41) ===
: This field lay in the southeastern part of Claragh, lying alongside the west bank of the river Bann, and a half mile or so northeast of the town of Kilrea. It comprised 7 acres 0 roods 25 perches, and was held as follows:
: – 1858-10-06: possessed jointly by William McKay [jun.] and his brother, Marshall McKay. <ref name="griffiths-william" />
: – 1864–1866: held jointly by the representatives of the late William McKay [jun.] and by James McKay, son of Marshall McKay (who died in 1860).
: – 1866: held jointly by the representatives of the late William McKay [jun.] and by Eliza McKay, widow of James McKay (who died in 1864).
: – 1866–1871: held solely by Dr, John McKay, son of Robert McKay [putative first cousin to William, jun., and Marshall McKay].
: – 1871–1879: held by Eliza McKay, widow of the late James McKay.
: – 1870–1899: held by Elizabeth McKay, sister of William and Marshall McKay.
: – 1899–1910: held by James Stinson.
: – 1910: purchased in fee by James Stinson.
: – 1910–1920: held in the name of James Stinson (who died in 1910).
: – 1920: The parcel went out of the McKay family when it was purchased by Hugh A. McIlrath. <ref name="vrb" />

=== Claragh townland (OS ref. 68) ===
: This field lay in the southern portion of Claragh, just west of the parcel enumerated above. It comprised 7 acres 0 roods 15 perches, and was held as follows:
: – 1858-10-06: landholder: William M'Kay [jun.] (<ref name="griffiths-william" />
: – 1864–1868: held by John McKay, William's younger brother.
: – 1868–1899: held by Elizabeth McKay, sister to William and John.
: – 1899: This parcel went out of the McKay family's hands when the lease was taken over by James McIntyre. <ref name="vrb" />

=== Notes re: lands held ===
* All land area stated in terms of English statute measure.
* All holdings were let by the Mercers Company of London, unless the parcel was sub-let to a sub-tenant by the lessee.
* Griffith's = Griffith's Valuation, completed in the parish of Kilrea on 6th October 1858.
* VRB = Valuation Revision Book, of which there are several. These Valuation Revision Books detail the changes in tenancy and the holding itself from 1864–1929.
* Land holdings often extended past the date of death, pending administration of an estate.

== Death and Will ==

: Miss Elizabeth McKay died at Kilrea on 21st February 1898, in her eighty-second year.<ref name="death" /> 

: She predeceased her brother, [[McKay-8629|Dr. Charles McKay]], by just seventeen days.<ref>''The Daily Telegraph'' (Sydney), 11 March 1898 (pg. 1). Death notice: "McKay.—March 10th, at his son's residence, 11 Cambridge-st., Stanmore, Charles McKay, M.D., in his 77th year." Online at Trove, hosted by the National Library of Australia, trove.nla.gov.au (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-06-08).</ref> Elizabeth and Charles were the last surviving of their siblings. In fact, Charles had bequeathed to Elizabeth the residue of his estate, that is, to take effect after the death of his wife.<ref>New South Wales. Will Books, 1800–1952. ''Last will and testament of Charles McKay, Doctor of Medicine, of Sydney in the Colony of New South Wales'', who died 10th March 1898; date of will: 11th March 1884; probate granted to Ellen McKay of Sydney, widow, on 25th July 1910. Bequests of his real and personal estate to his wife, Ellen, and the rest and residue of said estate to his sister, Elizabeth McKay, of Kilrea, county Londonderry, Ireland. Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk (extract by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-06-25).</ref> However, as fate would have it, that legacy was nullified by Elizabeth's earlier death.

: By her last will and testament, written on 18th February and proved in court a few weeks later on 11th March, Elizabeth left bequests of £12 "free of  legacy duty" to her niece, Margaret Smiley of Coleraine-street in Kilrea, widow [for whom, see research note, below], and the residue of her real and personal property to her nephew (her late sister Matilda's son), James Stinson, who lived with her in Church-street. She nominated her nephew to be the executor. Witnesses to the will included the Rev. A.E. Sixsmith, rector of the parish church in Kilrea (St. Patrick's Church of Ireland) and J.T. Dripps, merchant.<ref name="will">Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (Belfast). ''Will Calendars''. Index entry: Elizabeth McKay, registry: Londonderry, died 21st February 1898, date of grant: 11th March 1898, effects £275, abstract: "M'Kay late of Kilrea County Londonderry Spinster who died 21 February 1898 granted at Londonderry to James Stinson of Kilrea Farmer.” Index entry and digital images online at apps.proni.gov.uk (extract by Alison Kilpatrick, 2022-06-15).</ref>

* Family connection to Margaret Smiley:—In her last will and testament, Elizabeth McKay cited Margaret Smiley of Coleraine-street as her niece.<ref name="will" /> A connection to the McKay family has not been found to date. However, for others' reference, Margaret Smiley was the daughter of Thomas Hunter of Kilrea, shoemaker. On 28th June 1859, Margaret married John Smiley of Coleraine, son of Samuel Smiley, and a flax dealer by trade.<ref>General Register Office, Ireland. ''Civil Registration of a Marriage''. Index entry: Charles McKay died in Petersham district in 1898, father: not stated, mother: Margaret, registration no. 2987/1898 (accessed 2022-06-08).</ref> His body was buried in Rookwood Cemetery, Sydney. <ref name="burial" />

: The ''Dubbo Dispatch and Wellington Independent'' (New South Wales) noticed the death:
::    ''One of the oldest directors of the Sydney Hospital, Dr. Charles M'Kay, died at his son's residence, Cambridge-street, Stanmore, on Thursday. Dr. M'Kay, who was a native of Ireland, took his M.D. degree at St. Andrew's University, and was also a L.R.C.S. of Edinburgh. He came to this colony over forty years ago, and was for many years partner with Dr. M'Kellar, father of the Hon. C. M'Kellar, M.L.C., in practice in Lower George-street. In 1874, Dr. M'Kay was elected one of the directors of the Sydney Hospital, he having then held the position of hon. surgeon to the institution for a number of years. After serving ten years as hon. surgeon, Dr. M'Kay resigned the position, and was elected one of the hon. consulting surgeons to the hospital, a position he held till the time of his death. Dr. M'Kay was a member of the house and ward committees of the hospital, and during the twenty-two years he was on the board was one of the most regular attendants and hardest workers on behalf of the institution. At one time the deceased gentleman was possessed of a considerable amount of property, and many young medical men had to thank him for assistance, both financial and other; but later in life he met with several reverses, which somewhat crippled his resources. In January, 1896, Dr. M'Kay resigned his position on the board of directors owing to illness, and he has since been confined to his bed with paralysis. === Career notes ===

Citing a petition by Charles M'Kay, M.D., M.R.C.S., Edinburgh of 38, George-street North, for the position of third surgeon in the infiirmary. Online at Trove, hosted by the National Library of Australia, trove.nla.gov.au (accessed 2022-06-08).</ref> The ''Londonderry Standard'' noticed this achievement:
::    ''University Honour.—The Senatus Academicus of the University of St. Andrew's, after a strict examination, held in the University on the 1st of August, instant, conferred the degree of M.D. on Mr. Charles M'Kay of Kilrea. Mr. M'Kay holds also the diploma of the Royal College of Surgeons, Edinburgh, which he obtained on the 3d of May, 1843''.  <ref>''Londonderry Standard'', 16 August 1843 (pg. 2). "University Honour." Citing Charles M'Kay of Kilrea, having earned M.D. at St. Andrew's and the diploma of the R.C.S., Edinburgh. Digital image online at FindMyPast.co.uk, per The British Library Board (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 25 June 2022).</ref>
* Returned to Ireland to practice medicine at Kilrea. <ref name="medical-gazette-obit" /> <ref>''Isaac Slater's Commercial Directory of Ireland'' (1846). Digital images online at FindMyPast.co.uk (accessed 9 May 2022).</ref>

Online at Trove, hosted by the National Library of Australia, trove.nla.gov.au (transcript by Alison Kilpatrick, 8 June 2022).</ref>

=== Vintner===
* In 1859, purchased the Minchinbury Estate, then comprising 1220 acres, for £2000. The estate lay in and around Rooty Hill, about 43km. west of Sydney. <ref name="blacktown-memories" /> <ref name="historical-encounters">''Historical Encounters''. "Rooty Hill."Online at www.historicalencounters.org/he/rooty-hill/ (accessed 25 June 2022)</ref> <ref name="wikipedia-minchinbury">[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minchinbury,_New_South_Wales Wikpedia: Minchinbury, New South Wales].</ref>
* During the 1860s, Dr. McKay became one of the largest landowners in the area west of Sydney, holding 20,110 acres. <ref name="wikipedia-minchinbury" />
* In 1870, earned an honorable mention for his Madeira 1868, a white, full-bodied, and dry wine; grapes grown at Eastern Creek, Minchinbury. <ref>''The Sydney Morning Herald'', 9 July 1870 (p. 7). "Award of Prizes for Colonial Wines." Citing, amongst many others, the 1868 Madeira by Charles McKay, M.D., at Minchinbury.  Digital image online at Trove, hosted by the National Library of Australia, trove.nla.gov.au (accessed 25 June 2022).</ref>
* In 1872, his white wine, vintage 1869 or younger, adjudged too light for the class. <ref>''The Sydney Morning Herald'', 27 February 1872 (p. 2). "New South Wales Wines." Citing, amongst several others, the white wine of Charles McKay, M.D. Digital image online at Trove, hosted by the National Library of Australia, trove.nla.gov.au (accessed 25 June 2022).</ref>
* In 1879, sued Mr. John Wright to recover £2000 for damages alleged to be committed by Wright's cattle on the Minchinbury Estate at Eastern Creek, near Penrith; verdict recorded for the plaintiff with £38 for damages. <ref>''Evening News'' (Sydney), 11 February 1879 (p. 3). "Banco Court. ... M'Kay ''v''. Wright." Citing a suit brought by Dr. Charles McKay against Mr. John Wright for alleged damages by Mr. Wright's cattle upon the Minchinbury estate. Digital image online at Trove, hosted by the National Library of Australia, trove.nla.gov.au (accessed 25 June 2022).</ref>
* In 1881, put the Minchinbury Estate —Dr. McKay's "celebrated vineyard"— up for sale, owing to financial difficulties. In addition to the 1200 acres in Minchinbury, the property included Lucan Park, 321 acres, and 600 acres in several adjoining parcels of land. <ref>''The Sydney Morning Herald'', 9 August 1881 (p. 9). "Preliminary Intimation. Important Sale of Freehold Property. Citing the sale of Minchinbury Estate, Lucan Park, and adjoining parcels by Dr. Charles McKay. Digital image online at Trove, hosted by the National Library of Australia, trove.nla.gov.au (accessed 25 June 2022).</ref>
* c.1891, donated land at Rooty Hill where the Pioneer Memorial Church was subsequently built. <ref name="historical-encounters" /><ref name="wikipedia-minchinbury" />
* In 1895, the sale of the Minchinbury Estate and other lands finally sold, to James Angus. <ref name="wikipedia-minchinbury" />

=== Legacy ===
: Today, a portion of Charles' McKay's land at Mount Druitt, comprising 15 hectares, is known as Dr Charles McKay Reserve. <ref>[https://www.google.ca/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=&cad=rja&uact=8&ved=2ahUKEwir0fjB0sj4AhVEUM0KHWMnDGUQFnoECA4QAQ&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.blacktown.nsw.gov.au%2Ffiles%2Fassets%2Fpublic%2Fenvironment%2Freserve-plans-of-management%2Fdr-charles-mckay-reserve-plan-of-management.pdf&usg=AOvVaw38Ww3j-WsOc0ylvk3LWqPB Plan of Management for Dr Charles McKay Reserve, Mt Druitt."] Prepared by Urban Bushland Management Consultants Pty. Ltd., for Blacktown City Council, December 2007.) — ''Please note that this source is linked to a downloadable pdf document''.</ref>

[[Category:Islandmagee DNA Group Project]]
[[Category:Kildollagh Parish, County Londonderry]]
== Biography ==

Margaret was born in 1869 in Turnakibbock, Kildollagh, County Londonderry, Ireland, the 4th daughter of [[Taggart-2009|James Taggart]], a farmer, and [[Stewart-53456|Margaret Stewart]].<ref>Ireland Civil Registration Birth Index https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/birth_returns/births_1869/03377/2237803.pdf</ref>  Sarah as another given name from the birth registration of her daughter Isabel<ref> [https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/birth_returns/births_1907/01702/1675065.pdf Irish Civil Registration Daughter Isabel]</ref>. Also, multiple records refer to her as Maggie.

In 1892 she married [[Donaldson-5546|Campbell Thompson Dixon Donaldson]] in St James' Presbyterian Church, Ballymoney, County Antrim. He was a school teacher from Islandmagee and she was from Culbrim, Ballymoney.. The witnesses were [[Donaldson-714|James Hill Donaldson]] and Bella Taggart.<ref>Ireland Civil Registration Marriage Index https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1892/10638/5876104.pdf</ref>

In 1901 she was living in Kilcoan More, Islandmagee with her husband, a National School teacher, and their 3 children. She was a 27 year old general draper<ref>1901 Ireland Census https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1901/Antrim/Islandmagee/Kilcoanmore/990136/</ref>

In 1911 the family had moved to Balloo, Islandmagee with her husband, still a National School teacher and now with 4 children. She is 38 years old but no longer has a recorded occupation. The couple have been married for 18 years and 4 of their 5 children are still alive.<ref>1911Ireland Census https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1911/Antrim/Island_Magee/Balloo/188088/</ref>

20171916.Name: Stuart-4680
20171916.bio:
== Biography ==
James was born in 1743. He was the son of [[Stuart-3901|Irwin Stuart]] and [[McDaniel-4792|Elizabeth McDaniel]]. Married Grace Lynd of Stewartstown, Co Tyrone, daughter of William Lynd and Margaret Templeton. Built Gracehill House around 1776 and planted 100 beech trees along the drive. He raised a Yeomanry Corps (2nd Dunluce) to suppress Rebellion of 1798. Found on a website (cited): "On Saturday 9 June 1798, Lord Henry Murray, Colonel of the 2nd Royal Manx Fencibles marched out from Coleraine Barracks with part of his own corps, the Dunluce Cavalry led by Captain Macnaghten and the Dunluce Infantry led by Captain Stewart of Gracehill as well as two field pieces." Appointed Under Sheriff of County Antrim 10 Feb 1778.   He passed away in 1824.

42060965.bio:
== Biography ==
'''Hugh Glasgow''' was born on 8 September 1769 in East Nottingham Township, Chester County, Pennsylvania. He was the son of '''[[Glasgow-2871|John Glasgow]]''' and Mary Cranmer Glasgow.

Hugh was successful in agricultural pursuits before studying law. He was admitted to the bar and practiced law in Peach Bottom, Pennsylvania. From 1800 to 1813, he served as a judge in York County, Pennsylvania.

In 1813, he was elected as a '''Democratic-Republican''' to represent Pennsylvania's 4th congressional district in the U.S. House of Representatives. He served in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Congresses from 4 March 1813 to 3 March 1817. Shortly after leaving Congress, he passed away at the age of 48 on 31 January 1818 in Peach Bottom, Pennsylvania. He was interred at Slate Ridge Burying Ground.

=== Family ===
Hugh Glasgow was married twice:
* '''Elizabeth "Betsy" Ramsay Glasgow''' (1774–1802)
* '''Maria "Mary" Ramsay Glasgow''' (1779–1870) (m. 1804)

He was the father of the following children:
* '''Cunningham Sample Glasgow''' (1797–1798)
* '''John Neeper Glasgow''' (1799–1873)

== Biography ==
: Adam Kilpatrick ''alias''  Kirkpatrick lived in Lislea townland in the parish of Kilrea, county Londonderry. <ref name="tithe">Church of Ireland. Photocopies obtained from the PRONI, Belfast (2014); digital images online at www.nidirect.gov.uk (accessed 2021-06-20).</ref> <ref>Presbyterian Church of Ireland. Kilrea First Congregation, Kilrea, County Londonderry. ''Solemnization of a Marriage''. Microfilm copies held by the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (Belfast); archival ref. MIC1P/87. Transcribed by Barbara Braswell (Autumn, 2002); posted to the Bann Valley genealogy mailing list 2002-10-12 (hosted by Richard Torrens) (accessed Autumn 2002), archived online at www.torrens.org.uk/ListArchives/4qd-bannvalley/2002-October.txt.</ref> He also had some connection, whether a tenement or plot of farm land, in the town or townland of Kilrea. <ref>Presbyterian Church of Ireland. Kilrea First Congregation, Kilrea, County Derry.'' Solemnization of a Marriage''. Extract: Martha Kirpatrick [sic], daughter of late Adam Kirpatrick and Mary Gordon, of Lislea and Kilrea, to William White, jun. of Fallahogy [parish of Kilrea], son of William White, sen. and Serah [sic] Gibson.
